speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The Clerk of the House laid upon the table the 47th report of the clerk of petitions stating that he had examined the following petition presented on the 9th instant by Mr. Stewart, viz:- of Hugh Kirkpatrick, of Nanaimo, B.C., and allegedly 500,966 other Canadians, praying that the British North America Act be amended by inserting therein a bill of rights; and finds that all the requirements of standing order 68 have been complied with.

subtopic: HUGH KIRKPATRICK AND OTHERS-BILL OF RIGHTS-POINT OP ORDER, MR. DORION- RULING, MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. The rules concerning the presentation of petitions are found in standing order 68, section 7 of which reads as follows
On the next day following the presentation of a petition the Clerk of the House shall lay upon the table the report of the clerk of petitions upon the petitions presented and such report shall be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of that day. Every petition so reported upon, not containing matter in breach of the privileges of this house and which, according to the standing orders or practice of this house, can 'be received, shall then be deemed to be permitted to be read and received.
My contention is that this petition contains irregularities that make it non-receivable. The practice of this house to which section 7 which I have quoted refers is well defined in paragraph 591 of "Beauchesne" third edition, which reads:
The language of a petition should be respectful and temperate and free from disrespect to the Sovereign, or offensive imputation upon the character and conduct of parliament, or the courts of justice, or other tribunal, or constituted authority.
I refer Your Honour to the fourth paragraph of the petition, which reads as follows:
That recent experiences of Jehovah's Witnesses in the province of Quebec prove that throughout the whole dominion basic personal rights are open to attack and loss because of a failure to have them guaranteed by a written constitution.
The words "recent experiences in the province of Quebec" cannot mean anything else than the legal proceedings that were instituted against Jehovah's Witnesses. Therefore this paragraph constitutes an offensive imputation upon the character and conduct of the courts

of justice, which, as is well known, have already rendered decisions on the conduct of Jehovah's Witnesses.
There is another reason why this petition is irregular. It is also a well known fact that matters pertaining to the conduct of Jehovah's Witnesses are at the present time under consideration by some tribunals, namely, courts of the sessions of the peace and the Supreme Court of Canada. Therefore, as it is a matter sub judice, it should not form the subject of a petition before the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: HUGH KIRKPATRICK AND OTHERS-BILL OF RIGHTS-POINT OP ORDER, MR. DORION- RULING, MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
I should like first of all to say to' the hon. member that I am very grateful to him for being kind enough to advise me of his intention to raise a point of order today when the report of the clerk of petitions came before the house, because it gave me an opportunity to study the matter.
The petition of Hugh Kirkpatrick of Nanaimo, British Columbia, and 500,966 other Canadians was presented in the house on the 9th instant by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). Paragraph 4 thereof reads as follows:
That recent experiences of Jehovah's Witnesses in the province of Quebec prove that throughout the whole dominion basic personal rights are open to attack and loss because of a failure to have them guaranteed by a written constitution.
The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) takes exception to this allegation on the ground that there is now before the courts of the province of Quebec a case connected with the activities of Jehovah's Witnesses in that province. The hon. member's contention is that the matter, being sub judice, cannot be dealt with on the floor of the House of Commons.
I have failed to find any authority or precedent justifying the contention that a petition cannot be received on the ground that it refers to matters before the courts. There is no reflection on the courts of Quebec in the statement that recent experiences prove that personal rights are open to attack and loss. As a matter of fact I am inclined to think that, as long as the case on trial is not discussed but only referred to, a petition referring to it is quite in order. The prohibition referring to sub judice matters applies particularly to debates but it cannot curtail a citizen's right to present a petition. All authorities agree that the right of petitioning parliament for redress of grievances is acknowledged as a fundamental principle of the constitution. It has been uninterruptedly exercised from very early times and has had a profound effect in determining the main forms of parliamentary

Questions
procedure. The historical aspects of petitioning were originally directed to judicial rather than legislative remedies.
In 1669, the Commons of England passed a resolution declaring that it is the inherent right of every commoner to prepare and present petitions to the House of Commons in case of grievances and the House of Commons to receive the same; that it is an undoubted right and privilege to judge and determine, touching the nature and matter of such petitions, how far they are fit and unfit to be received. The mere mention of recent experiences in the province of Quebec with respect to personal rights is not sufficient to deprive petitioners of their right to request that the British North America Act be amended so as to empower parliament to pass a federal bill of rights in order to secure freedom of speech, press and worship to all people in Canada. The report of the clerk of petitions is in order in the statement that all the requirements of standing order 68 have been complied with and there can be no objection to the petition being received.

TRADE MISSION TO CHINA
speechtext:
1.	Has any trade mission gone to China, and with what results, and is there yet any improvement in the economic conditions of that country?
2.	Is the government aware of the trade treaty recently made with America by China, and is a similar trade treaty under way on behalf of Canada with China, or is one 'being sought there yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRADE MISSION TO CHINA
speechtext:
1.	No trade mission has been sent to China, but Canada maintains in addition to the Canadian embassy at Nanking, a senior trade commissioner at Shanghai who is keeping the government constantly informed of trade conditions. Economic conditions remain very uncertain and trade greatly restricted without immediate prospects of improvement.
2.	A treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation between the United States of America and the Republic of China was signed on November 2, 1946. The treaty provides for the reciprocal most favoured nation treatment between the two countries.
A commercial modus vivendi between Canada and China was completed on September 26, 1946, in Nanking by an exchange of notes between the Chinese government and the Canadian ambassador to China. The modus vivendi provides for the reciprocal exchange of unconditional most favoured nation treatment. This means that the products of each country on importation into the other country will not be subject to customs duties or charges greater than those which apply to any third country. Similarly any concession which either Canada or China may grant in the future to a third country will be automatically extended to the other. Thus imports into Canada from China will be subject to the intermediate tariff and lower rates rather than the general tariff as heretofore. The tariff treatment which Canada affords to British countries is specifically excepted from the operation of the modus vivendi so that the British preferential system is not affected by it.

speechtext:
'I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. In view of recent press reports, and in particular

Inquiries oj the Ministry
a dispatch from Washington which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on June 17, regarding the delay in initiation of Canada's air service to Bermuda arising out of difficulty over use of the United States airport there, would the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply care to make a statement which would clarify this situation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES ARRANGEMENTS FOR SERVICE TO BERMUDA
speechtext:
The following statement has been prepared in answer to this inquiry.
The Canadian government has for long made no secret of its intention to operate an air service southward through Bermuda and the Caribbean area to Latin America. The necessary agreement has been reached with Bermuda and with Trinidad and Jamaica regarding traffic rights, and Trans-Canada Air Lines is anxious to initiate the service at the earliest possible day. In fact this service would have been in operation considerably before this time if it had not been for difficulties arising out of the use of Kindley field, which is the only available air base in Bermuda.
This base, along with certain others in British colonial possessions in the Caribbean, is a United States army base obtained in the destroyer-bases deal during the recent war. It is available for civil use by the United States and by the United Kingdom, of course, but the question of its civil use by the air lines of other countries was left for agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom, and until such agreement has been reached the civil aircraft of other countries are not, apparently, allowed to use the field.
The Canadian government, of course, made known a considerable time ago its desire to use Kindley field, and discussions between the United Kingdom and the United States have, we understand, taken place regarding civil use of this and other Ltnited States military airports in. British possessions farther south. We also understood that general agreement in principle had been reached between the United Kingdom and the United States on this subject. The United Kingdom has informed us that it would have no objection to immediate use of Kindley field by Trans-Canada Air Lines. However, we are informed that the United: States is unwilling to permit any temporary use of Kindley field by Trans-Canada Air Lines or the air lines of any country-other than the United States and the United Kingdom-until formal agreement with the United Kingdom regarding civil use of this and other bases concerned has been signed. We are also informed that
the United States does not wish to sign this agreement unless and until an agreement is signed covering similar use of United States military bases in Newfoundland. Negotiations between the Newfoundland commission of government, and the United States in this connection have been going on over a long period of months, but. no final agreement has as yet been reached. Meanwhile the United States has not- allowed Trans-Canada Air Lines to make use of the air base in Bermuda until it has reached agreement with Newfoundland regarding similar use of United States bases there as a prerequisite to signature of the United Kingdom-United States agreement regarding the base in Bermuda. Until that time, therefore, the Canadian air service to Bermuda and farther south must, much to our regret, be deferred.
We, of course, are not a direct party to any negotiations regarding the bases in Newfoundland, and all we have been able to do is to make known our hope that this matter may be cleared up speedily.

subtopic: RACE MEETINGS-ADMINISTRATION AND SUPERVISION OF PARI-MUTUEL BETTING
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the criminal code to give certain rights to people in this country to undertake and run pari-mutuels at different affairs throughout the land. I feel that this is a type of legislation which no hon. member should support, and I say that mainly because it gives to certain people in Canada the right to carry on pari-mutuels while it is discriminatory in that it prohibits other associations from undertaking dog racing and car racing.
I do not rise to support betting or parimutuels. I rise to protest against the fact that we have here a situation wherein wealthy people, race horse owners in this country, are given the right to carry on pari-mutuels at our fairs under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture. I submit that if the government sees fit to allow any type of gambling of this sort it should not pass an amendment such as this which, as I have pointed out, is discriminatory. On that ground also I protest. I feel that if we are to have a provision 
of this kind it should apply to other associations such as dog racing. They should have the same privilege.
In conclusion, I wish to protest the whole affair. I do not think that this house should pass such legislation at all.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved the second reading of Bill No. 339 to amend the Old Age Pensions Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Surely we shall have a statement from the minister before second reading.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I think all hon. members will agree with the leader of the opposition that the house will expect a comprehensive statement about this measure.
Mr. Speaker, the bill which is introduced by this resolution represents another forward step taken by the government of this country in the building of an adequate social security programme for the Canadian people. It has particular significance because of the fact that the legislation which is being amended by this bill represented, when it was passed in 1927, the first occasion on which the federal authority in this country assumed responsibilities of a permanent nature in the public assistance field. Prior to that date action had been taken with respect to labour legislation including the establishment of fair wage legislation and the provision of a scheme of government annuities. We have now had a continuous period of twenty years through which the federal authority has maintained, and indeed from time to time increased, its commitments with respect to the care of the needy aged in all parts of the dominion.
This government has given conclusive evidence of its concern for the welfare of the aged among our population. It was a government under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that first introduced the Old Age Pensions Act in 1927. Through the amendments and changes which have been made since that time up to the present, the intention of the government has been to make easier the lot of our older citizens who had need of financial assistance.

Old Age Pensions
It is important at this stage to recall the proposals the federal government made in August 1945 to the provinces with respect to a programme covering national health, public investment and social security. These proposals include a suggested scheme for a national old age pensions and old age assistance programme of a fundamental character.
What we do now must be consistent with the dominion government's proposals to the provinces. We have a plan and it is a good plan. What we do today must not in any way prejudice the over-all plan. I would remind the house that the proposals of the dominion government with regard to old age pensions, and indeed in the whole field of social security, remain an essential part of the government's programme as has been repeatedly stated by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and myself.
The Old Age Pensions Act of 1927 originally provided for a $20 monthly maximum pension totalling $240 a year, with an outside maximum income of $125 a year apart from the pension. I ask hon. members to bear these figures in mind in the light of what the government is now proposing in the present amendments.
Later amendments to the act were made which, without increasing the benefits to the pensioners themselves, relieved the provinces of a considerable share of the pension cost by increasing the federal government's percentage of contribution from 50 per cent to 75 per cent and correspondingly reducing the provincial share from 50 per cent to 25 per cent.
The first occasion on which the scope of the act itself was widened was when the then government of Canada, under the leadership of the present Prime Minister, introduced amendments to provide additional categories of pensioners, extending the benefits of old age pensions legislation to the blind.
In addition to this, since 1942 a number of the provinces have been paying supplementary allowances to pensioners in addition to payments made by the provinces and the federal government jointly under the Old Age Pensions Act itself. These payments have ranged in amount from nothing at all in some provinces up to $10 monthly in British Columbia.
In 1943, action was taken by this government under the War Measures Act to increase the maximum pension payable from $20 to $25 a month, and, a few months later, to increase the maximum income allowable under the act from $365 to $425 a year, inclusive of pension.
Finally, as a result of the meeting of the interprovincial old age pensions board in November. 1946, a complete revision of the
regulations under the Old Age Pensions Act was undertaken and made effective on May 15 of this year. These regulations are now considerably more generous than they were before, particularly in making it possible to set the commencement date of pension back to the month following application, and in respect to the interpretation of residence and the calculation of income. More generous provisions have also been included dealing with the kinds of evidence that can be accepted as proof of age. The effect of these new regulations, which relax the present restrictions applying to applicants for pension and to the circumstances under which pensions may be granted, will be to add an additional half a million dollars yearly to the cost of old age pensions.
I would point out, however, that the government has for some time now made clear its desire to introduce comprehensive and sweeping changes in the provision for the aged and the blind throughout this country. Hon. members know of the proposals which were advanced by the dominion government to the provinces in the conference of August, 1945. These proposals fall into three main categories-public investment, social security and tax reform.
As part of its programme in the field of social security, the federal government proposed a system of national old age pensions. This provided for the federal government to assume the full responsibility for paying pensions at the rate of $30 a month to all persons in Canada seventy years and over. The federal government proposed these pensions for all eligible persons without any income or means test whatsoever, and the federal government proposed to administer this scheme directly and bear 100 per cent of the cost, amounting to an estimated $200 million annually.
In addition to this, the federal government also undertook to pay, on a fifty-fifty basis with the provinces, the cost of pensions to the aged between the ages of sixty-five and seventy years and to the blind from the age of twenty-one. This was to be subject to a means test more generous than at present and was to be paid on a basis of $30 a month pension. The pro\ inces were, under this proposal, to administer this scheme and the cost of this part of the programme was estimated at a total of $34 to $40 million annually, with the federal government's share of this approximately $17 to $20 million annually.
This, in broad outline, represents the proposals made by the federal government to the provinces with respect to the aged and the blind. These are an integral part of the
Old Age Pensions

objectives in social security which this government has set for itself as soon as satisfactory over-all arrangements on social security, fiscal and other matters can be made with the provinces.
I mention these proposals at this point because I wish hon. members of this house to see not only the background of the various steps that have already been taken by the government of this country with respect to provisions actually in existence for the aged and the blind, but also the plans which we have laid before this country as to the direction in which, with the cooperation of the provinces, we hope to move.
The government has also indicated in its proposals to the provinces, and elsewhere, the advantages of a more strictly contributory system of old age insurance. The principal advantage of a contributory system is that, like the universal pension scheme, it offers payment as of right to persons reaching the established retirement age who have paid into a fund specifically created by joint contribution for that purpose. It removes the fear of destitution without impairing the dignity and self-respect of the person who reaches the later stages of life and is no longer able to maintain himself by his own earning effort.
In most respects, the contributory system of old age insurance shares common advantages with the universal pension scheme at seventy contained in the dominion's proposals to the provinces. To quote from the dominion government's proposals:
Payment of pension as of right to people of this age offers the best kind of economic security. It removes fear of destitution much more certainly than any other method, and relieves the old people of the necessity of seeking work, or of endeavouring to keep on working in unfavourable circumstances and beyond the age at which they should 'be able to retire, without dependence on charity or burdening the family. In addition to providing a minimum subsistence for those with no other resources, this system would enable other persons with moderate private savings to retire from active work sooner, or in more comfort, than would otherwise be possible.
I make reference to this inclusion in the explanatory features of the proposals made to the provinces to show that the government has in mind what the Prime Minister stated in this house a number of years ago to be ultimately the kind of pattern in respect of social insurance which we must envisage in this country. Admittedly in a country like ours, with great open spaces, a federal state, a contributory system along the lines I have been talking about is not as feasible as it is in some unitary states; and certainly the far-flung rural parts of our provinces do present difficulties in the consideration of such a 
scheme. My own belief is that we must ultimately look to the establishment of such a system, perhaps beginning in stages, and that our long range plans should be directed toward that desirable goal. It would therefore be a mistake-and I say this with all the seriousness that I know hon. members will recognize in my approach to this problem-to take any action now which would result in placing additional obstacles in the way of what I believe to be a desirable objective.
I have already said that in the consideration of this measure one must bear in mind the broad scheme of social security envisaged by the government in its proposals made to the provinces twenty-four months ago, and which, in its general objectives we believe meets the wishes of the great majority of the people of this country.
No greater disservice could be rendered to those who support the desirability of a broad social security system than to throw out of balance particular phases and destroy the desired ultimate pattern. That pattern is in the thoughts of the present administration now as it was when it laid before the provinces its objectives in the field of health, public investment and social security. I say with great respect that pattern hon. members should keep before themselves in the discussion of this measure. No one has stated that pattern in terms of general objectives better than the Prime Minister of Canada, who, speaking before the annual convention of the American Federation of Labour in Toronto on October 9, 1942, declared:
The era of freedom will be achieved only as social security and human welfare become the main concern of men and nations. It is necessary that social security and human welfare should be expressed in definite terms-of the kind of objectives I have in mind I would merely mention the following as a national minimum; useful employment for all who are willing to work, standards of nutrition and housing adequate to ensure the health of the whole population; social insurance against privations resulting from unemployment, accident, the death of the breadwinner, ill health and old age.
That, coming from a man whose whole life has been devoted to placing the general above the particular interest. I know will be accepted by this house as a serious statement of direction. Also this matter we are now discussing must be considered in the light of the solid and responsible basis which has been already provided for in the growing structure of social security which stage by stage we are building in this country. I am thinking in particular of the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940 which today protects from the hazards of unemployment over million Canadian workmen and serves as a major bulwark of

Old Age Pensions
social security. I am thinking also of the Family Allowances Act of 1944, also initiated by this government, which today brings to
3.600.000	Canadian children in 1,600,000 homes the means of ensuring better opportunities and a better standard of living. By this single measure alone we have been able to provide an increased measure of security to fully one-half of the total population of our country. Two-thirds of the entire population of Canada are benefited directly either by the protection afforded through unemployment insurance or by the increased social well-being offered through our family allowances legislation.
We must also take note of the important social security measures extended through the Department of Veterans Affairs, its grants for land and housing, its reestablishment credits, out-of-work benefits, retraining in vocational and trade schools; its underwriting of university courses for our veterans. The Department-of Veterans Affairs programme for the rehabilitation and reestablishment of veterans is the most generous and comprehensive that any country has provided for its servicemen and women, and forms a part of the structure of social security.
When one considers the extent and coverage of our present fourfold programme of unemployment insurance, family allowances and veterans legislation, and our present benefits for old age pensioners, together with what I am proposing in the amending bill, one recognizes the basis for the statement that fully three-fourths of the people of Canada today come directly under the protection of these four measures which we have established as the cornerstone of our social security structure in Canada.
The present Old Age Pensions Act which we are discussing today already provides assistance to something like forty per cent of our total aged population seventy years and over. The figures supplied to us by the provinces show that as of the end of March, 1947, no less than
209.000	aged persons and 7,000 blind persons were in receipt of pensions under the legislation as it exists today. This represents in some provinces as high as sixty per cent of the total aged population.
The measure which is being introduced today will make it possible for the provinces to increase by twenty per cent or more the assistance which has been given to date to this substantial section of our aged population. Where, because of outside income, pensioners have not been receiving the full pension, the
increase which the provinces will be enabled to give under the new legislation will be even greater than twenty per cent.
Of equal importance, if not greater, is the fact that because of the more generous provisions which are included in this amending bill respecting the amount of outside income which a pensioner may have and still remain on pension, thousands of persons will be brought for the first time within the benefits of our old age pensions legislation.
It is estimated that when the provinces have taken full advantage of the increases in maximum income allowable for aged and blind persons which are permitted by this proposed amending bill, the result will be an increase in the pension rolls of something between 60,000 and 65,000 additional persons. In other words, when this new bill becomes law in all the provinces, fully 50 per cent of the aged people of Canada will be receiving benefits under it, and that 50 per cent comprises that section of the aged population which can genuinely be said to be most in need of outside assistance.
The financial implications of this bill deserve the most careful consideration. The provincial supplemental allowances at present being paid -and there is nothing in this bill to prevent them from being continued-amount to well over six million dollars annually. If the provinces take full advantage of these new provisions, the provincial share of old age pensions under the act itself will advance from approximately sixteen million dollars to approximately twenty-three million dollars. This will automatically mean that the federal government's share of the cost of old age pensions will rise from forty-eight million dollars to sixty-eight million dollars a year. When this bill becomes law and full effect is given to it in all the provinces, this country will be spending on old age pensioners and blind persons close to one hundred million dollars a year.
Perhaps at this stage it would be of assistance to hon. members if I were to outline the main provisions of the amending bill.
1.	It is proposed, in this amending bill, to do away with the provision which has been in the act up to the present time, section 9(1), setting the maximum pension which any province is permitted to pay. Under these new amendments, therefore, the provinces themselves will be free to fix the maximum pension.
2.	The amount of income which a pensioner is permitted to have, inclusive of his pension, is increased in the case of a single aged person under the proposed bill from $425 to $600 annually. The practical effect of this will be that any province will be free, if it
Old Age Pensions

chooses to do so, to set a pension rate as high as $50 a month or $600 a year for a person who has no other income of his own with which to supplement his pension allotment.
In case of a married pensioner, this maximum income limit is set at $1,080 instead of $850 as at present.
In the case of a single blind pensioner the new amount of maximum income allowable will be including pension $720, whereas formerly it was $500.
In the case of a blind pensioner married to a sighted spouse, the maximum income limit is set at $1,200 whereas it was formerly $925.
In the case of two blind persons married and living together, the maximum allowable is set in the bill at $1,320.
In all of these cases the amounts mentioned are inclusive of any pension or pensions receivable by one or both spouses under the provisions of the act.
It will be seen therefore that this provision raises substantially the margins of outside income which an individual is permitted to have and still qualify for full or partial pension. Because of these higher income limits the number of aged and blind persons who will now be eligible for pension will be substantially increased. I have already stated that the department's estimate for this increase is about 60,000 additional pensioners, assuming of course that all the provinces will take full advantage of these higher income limits.

In this connection it is interesting to note that the federal contribution has risen by successive stages from $10 per month per pensioner in 1927 to $15 in 1931 to $18.75 in 1943 to $22.50 under this present bill. I said, apart from the provinces which are paying supplemental allowances. I shall have something to say about British Columbia in a few moments which might warm the heart of my hon. friend and colleague.
4.	Another feature of this new bill, which I ' am sure will commend itself favourably to all members of this house, involves a modification of the present residence requirements. At the present time the act states that a person must have lived in Canada for the twenty-year period immediately prior to application before he can be considered eligible for pension. While this requirement has been somewhat modified by regulation, cases of hardship still arise. Persons who were born in Canada and have lived here almost all their lives sometimes disqualify themselves for pension by moving within the twenty years, before applying for pension, to the United States or to some other country and remaining for periods in excess of the four-year limit permitted by the present regulations.
The amending bill makes provision to cover such cases. It provides that any gaps in Canadian residence during the twenty years prior to application may be compensated for by earlier periods of residence. These earlier periods of residence must be double in amount to the periods of absence during the twenty-year period before application. In other words, if a person makes application for old age pension at 70 years of age, and it is shown that he has been absent for ten years from Canada between his fiftieth and his seventieth birthday, it does not necessarily follow that that person is ineligible for pension. He can get a pension if he can prove that he resided in Canada prior to his fiftieth birthday for a period of twenty years. This provision thus compensates on a two-for-one basis for the ten-year absence from Canada during the latter portion of his life.
It is felt that this provision will enable the pension authorities, which under the act are

Old Age Pensions
the provinces, to deal with a significant number of cases where, under the present act, there has been obvious hardship on this score.
5.	Hon. members will also note that the requirement regarding national status has been eliminated by this amending bill. This is consistent with the provisions of the unemployment insurance and the family allowances acts, neither one of which limits eligibility for benefit in this way. It is felt that the requirement of twenty years' residence in Canada as a minimum provides an adequate safeguard.
I am sure there will be general agreement with the view that, as a matter of equity, any person who has spent twenty years or more of his working life in Canada and paid through taxes his full share towards the maintenance of public and other social services should not be debarred from application for old age pension when he reaches his declining years.
6.	One special change in respect to the blind should perhaps also be noted. The existing provision debarring blind persons who marry from receiving more than one pension between the two of them will now be eliminated. This provision was originally inserted to discourage persons suffering from hereditary types of blindness from marrying. While it is undoubtedly true that no one wishes to encourage the marriage of persons suffering from hereditary blindness, it is not felt that the existing provision has been particularly effective, nor is it felt that this represents the constructive approach to the solution of this problem. This problem should not be met by depriving a blind married couple of this subsistence which they require for their actual maintenance.
7.	There is one final change of importance which I have left to the last because it concerns the provinces much more than it does the federal authority. This change affects the determination of the province responsible for the payment of the provincial share of pension.
At the present time there is a complicated provision which says that the provincial share of pension shall be divided proportionately between those provinces in which the pensioner has resided during the twenty-year period prior to his application for pension. For example a pensioner may reside in British Columbia but his twenty years of residence prior to coming on pension might be divided between eight years in British Columbia, six years in Saskatchewan, four years in Quebec and two years in Prince Edward Island. British Columbia has to bill each of the three other provinces for their respective shares of
the $6.25 monthly, which is the provincial portion of the pension. This is an obviously cumbersome method of apportioning provincial costs, especially since for most provinces these amounts paid out and the amounts received from other provinces balance off fairly evenly in the long run.
This amending bill introduces a simpler method of apportioning the provincial cost. It provides that the entire provincial share shall be paid by the province in which the pensioner has lived for the greatest number of days in the three-year period prior to his reaching pensionable age or prior to making application for pension, whichever is the later.
Needless to say the provinces have been consulted on this change, as they have indeed been advised of the intentions of this government with respect to the principles involved in the other proposed changes in the act.
I should like to have it noted that as a result of the bill, the contribution to pensions for the aged offered by the federal government represents an increase of 125 per cent over the contribution originally offered under the Old Age Pensions Act of 1927.
The bill provides in permanent legislative form for an increase of $10 in the amount of pension at present authorized under the Old Age Pensions Act itself. This is so because the order in council authorizing a .$5 supplementary payment was never incorporated in the Old Age Pensions Act itself and will expire when the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act runs its course within the year. The bill, therefore, incorporates this supplementary payment, and the pension payable under the act is increased by $10.
But the bill actually does more than that. It does not merely make it possible for the provinces to raise the pension to $30 a month. By removing the pension ceiling and by increasing the federal contribution, the government is, in fact, opening the wav for the provinces to pay more than $30 a month. If the six provinces which are now paying supplemental allowances continue to do so, the result will be a pension in most parts of Canada substantially in excess of the standard rate of $30 a month, and this in most cases without an additional - cent of expense per pensioner to the provinces.
Take the case of Alberta, for example. This province is already paying a combined pension and supplemental allowance amounting to $30 a month. Of this amount the Alberta government is currently paying $11.25, made up as follows: $6.25 a month as Alberta's share of the $25 pension provided by the federal law and wartime orders in council, and an additional provincial bonus of $5 a month
Old Age Pensions

which has been paid since 1942. The federal share payable at the present time is $18.75 a month, which, under the provisions of this amending bill, will be increased to $22.50 a month. If Alberta does no more than continue its present payment from provincial funds amounting to $11.25 a month, this sum, together with the increased federal contribution of $22.50, will mean that Alberta can actually raise its pension rate to $33.75 a month without an additional cent of cost per pensioner to the province over what it is paying at the present time.
Exactly the same situation, and I know there will be special interests in this, prevails in Saskatchewan.

No bill which this parliament can pass can in any way affect what a province may do within its own constitutional jurisdiction. What applies to Alberta applies in equal measure to Saskatchewan. The house will recall that the government made known in January of this year its intention as to amending the act. Saskatchewan is now, since April of this year, paying a combined pension and allowance of $30 monthly, the provincial share consisting of the $6.25 a month which represents the province's part of the combined federal-provincial old age pension and, in addition to this, a $5 supplemental allowance. This means that the provincial contribution from these two sources currently amounts to $11.25 monthly. With the increase in the federal contribution from $18.75 to $22.50 provided in this amending bill, it will now be possible for Saskatchewan to pay a pension as high as $33.75 a month without an additional cent of cost per pensioner to the province over what it is paying at the present time.
Turning now to the province of British Columbia, we find that there the province which started to pay a provincial supplement of $5 monthly in 1942 is now paying a provincial supplement of $10 a month, in addition to the sum of $6.25 a month representing the provincial share of the combined federal-provincial old age pension. In other words, the provincial contribution here amounts currently to $16.25 a month compared to the federal contribution of $18.75 a month which, under this amending bill, will be increased to $22.50 a month. This will mean that the

province of British Columbia will be enabled by this legislation to pay a pension as high as $38.75 a month without an additional cent of cost per pensioner to the province over what it is paying at the present time.
Ontario is paying a somewhat smaller pension and allowance, not exceeding $28 a month. It too provides a provincial supplement over and above its statutory contribution of $6.25 a month under the federal-provincial old age pension plan. This contribution in Ontario is a variable one, being 15 per cent of the actual amount of pension being paid, up to a maximum of $3 per month in any one case. In other words, the maximum provincial contribution to any pension at the present time is $9.25 a month, consisting of the $6.25 monthly contribution .which is required of the province under the federal-provincial old age pension plan and the additional $3 provincial supplement. Since this amending bill calls for an increase in the federal contribution from $18.75 to $22.50 a month, it will be possible for the province of Ontario, by maintaining its current rate of contributions, to pay a pension of $31.75 a month without increasing its current expenditures per pensioner on old age pensions.
In summary, it will be apparent that the result of the present amending bill will be in effect to set a standard minimum pension of $30 per month in all the provinces, assuming, of course, that all the provinces will be anxious to take full advantage of the federal contribution. More than this, however, it will undoubtedly result in a number, and perhaps even a majority, of the provinces of Canada going beyond this $30 pension to set higher pension rates in their respective provinces. The illustrations I have just given make it clear that in a substantial number of cases the provinces will be able to do this without increasing in any way the commitments that they have made already, on their own initiative, with respect to the limits of their contributions to old age pensions at the present time. Nothing in the federal Old Age Pensions Act as it will be amended by this present bill debars any of these provinces from incorporating their present provincial supplements into their basic pension rates, and it is thought that the provinces already pajdng provincial supplements will, in fact, be encouraged to maintain their provincial contributions on at least the present basis. If this is done, the result will be that we will have in actual fact a pension rate throughout all of Canada which, on the average, will

Old Age Pensions
exceed substantially the standard pension rate of $30 contemplated by these present amendments.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that after consideration of this measure the house will conclude that this bill goes a long way towards easing the lot of our aged people and those who have been afflicted with blindness. It is a progressive and advancing step. It will aid and assist both the present pensioners and those who will, for the first time, become eligible for pension. What this bill will accomplish, if the provinces take full advantage of its provisions, may be summarized in this way:
1.	It does away with the provision limiting the maximum pension which any province is permitted to pay.
2.	It establishes a basic standard pension of $30 a month to which the dominion will contribute and leaves the provinces free to increase the standard pension rate as they deem advisable.
3.	It raises the statutory pension to which the dominion will contribute from $20 to $30 a month.
4.	It increases substantially the amount of outside income which a pensioner may have and still qualify for full or partial pension.
5.	It increases the amount of allowable income for a single aged person, from $425, inclusive of pension, to $600 a year.
6. It increases the maximum allowable income for a married old age pensioner from $850, inclusive of pension, to $1,080 a year.
7. It increases the maximum allowable income for an old age pensioner married to a blind person from $925, inclusive of pension, to $1,200 a year.
8. It increases the maximum allowable income for a single blind pensioner from $500, inclusive of pension, to $720 a year.

The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said that no member of this house has any monopoly of interest in the aged people of this country. I believe that to be a correct statement. The government is very much aware of the need for improving the lot of our aged people. Our older citizens are the people who have built this country and made it the nation it is today. I firmly believe this parliament will recognize that it has a solemn obligation towards those who on reaching the later years find themselves in need of assistance in maintaining themselves.
What we do now-Ind I cannot emphasize this too strongly-must be consistent both with present need and the need of tomorrow. It must be consistent with what we are trying to achieve with the joint cooperation of the provinces. It must be consistent with the ultimate realization of a self-sustaining and nation-wide contributory system of retirement insurance.
In conclusion I should like to summarize the objectives and the general nature of these proposals made by this government two years ago, particularly in relation to the establishment of a national health programme and a national social security programme, because they are inextricably intertwined and interwoven with the matter that we are now discussing. The national health programme as laid down by the federal government included financial assistance to the provinces in establishing health insurance, to provide health services to individuals, health grants to assist and extend public health and preventive medicine, a grant for organization and planning of medical services, and provision for low interest loans for the construction of hospitals. I prefer to finish my statement.
The measure which is today being placed before hon. members of this house for consideration has been dehberately designed to keep within the frammvork of the dominion's proposals to the provinces on assistance to the aged, so that it may be abundantly clear that we are not offering this measure to the house and to the country as a substitute for the proposals themselves, but rather, indeed, as a forward step taken to provide a greater measure of assistance to the aged at the present time, but taken in a manner that will be completely consistent with the proposals and within the broad framework of the social security objectives that the government enunciated therein.
Ten governments of Canada today-federal and provincial-by establishing ministries of health and public welfare, have indicated their acceptance of the fact that the provision of public welfare services is an essential responsibility of government in a modern democratic society.
Canada is already in the forefront of nations who seek to raise social standards and) protect the wage earner and the family, the veteran, the farmer and the needy aged. We can only proceed by progressive stages and it is as an additional stage that I present this bill today.
We have set our hand to the attainment of long-range social objectives. Upon the attain-

ment of those objectives a great deal depends not only for the present day but for the future.
The task of this government in cooperation with the provinces is to provide for the welfare of the nation as a whole. It is with this in mind that the government has made clear its objectives in regard to national health, social security, public investment.
National programmes of such a broad and fundamental nature cannot be achieved in a country like Canada only by the central government. They can be achieved by all governments, dominion and provincial, acting in cooperation to ensure the greatest possible measure of well-being, economic security and social welfare for the Canadian people.
This present measure, representing as it does a joint cooperative effort of the dominion and the provinces, brings us one step nearer to the achievement of the objective that we seek-all governments alike-the greatest measure of security for all the people of Canada, in whatever part of this great country they may live.

I say, Mr. Speaker, that the measure has been too long delayed by far, both in this session and in previous years, and it provides only partial justice to the aged. The third criticism, an important one, is that the measure is a complete reversal of the government's policy as announced two years ago. Now, another point. Two years ago this government proposed an old age assistance plan to apply to persons from 65 to 69 years of age, a joint plan to which the dominion and the provinces would contribute. There is nothing in this measure providing assistance for persons between the ages of 65 and 69. And I suggest there should be particularly for widows between those ages; they form a class of people who need assistance at this time. It should apply to persons between those ages. My fourth criticism is that the measure gives no consideration at all to blind persons under 40 years of age-none whatever. I suggest that if there is any justification for aiding blind persons over 40, if there is justification for increasing assistance to them, there is justification for some assistance to blind persons of 39, 38, 37 and lower ages.
I have one other observation to make and a question to ask. In the original old age pensions bill there was no assistance for the first inhabitants of the country, the Indians. They were excluded. That exclusion is continued in this measure. I would ask the government to state its policy with respect to this particular group of people.
I wish now to make a brief statement on the historical background of this measure. As
Old Age Pensions

the minister said, it was in 1927 that legislation relating to old age pensions was first enacted in Canada. In that year this parliament passed an act which enabled the dominion government to negotiate agreements with one or more of the provinces by which the dominion and the provinces would each pay fifty per cent of the pension provided that the age of seventy years had been reached. The dominion government prescribed in this legislation that the pension itself was to be limited to $20 per month. The minister today says the provinces can increase the amount beyond what the dominion pays. Some members raised the question-and it could not be denied-that under the bill the provinces can also lessen the amount they pay. Under the original bill they were required to pay, first, half the cost, and then 25 per cent of the cost.

That was the condition. Those are simple statements of fact in the record.
I might point out the order in which the provinces came into the scheme. The dominion came along and said, "We will pay half the cost of this plan in any province where the province will pay the other half under these conditions." The provinces came in in the following order:	British Columbia
in 1927-

It was after British Columbia and after Manitoba. In 1931 a major change was made in the act, namely, in the distribution of the costs. The dominion then began to assume seventy-five per cent of the cost and the provinces twenty-five per cent. And in 1937 the blind over forty years of age were made eligible for the pension scheme. For twenty years there has been no statutory revision of the amount of pension paid; in fact, there had been no financial revision of any kind until the war came along, and then by order in council, I think in 1943, provision .was made for a $5 increase a month. That increase which was made possible by dominion order in council did not precede but followed the action of certain provinces. Certain provinces went ahead on their own to make increases when they found the dominion only slowly recognizing its responsibilities.
During these years almost all other incomes have increased in this country. From 1939 until the present time the cost of living has increased from 22 to 25 per cent; I am calling on my memory there. Industrial wages have increased by about 25 per cent. Many other wages and incomes have increased. This government itself made provision for increasing the incomes of members of parliament by $2,000 a year. Yet in that whole period of time only $5 a month or $60 a year increase was made for the old people, and now $60 more a year is being added to their income.
As I said, after the war the provinces and not the dominion began to take action in increasing the amount to be paid. British Columbia and Alberta in 1942 passed legislation authorizing increases. Early in 1943 Manitoba- and Nova Scotia took similar action. The dominion government in August 1943 passed an order in council by which pensions payable could be increased by $60 a year, or $5 a month; but the dominion provided also that the amount of other income which could be received by the pensioner had to be reduced by a similar amount. I am glad to see that today the government is changing that attitude.

Old Age Pensions
I wish to go back to these detailed criticisms. I said this measure had been too long delayed. I pointed out that it is twenty years since it first came in, that there was no change in the rate of pension until the war was half over, and then only So a month. Now the minister brings in a measure which goes only one-tenth of the way toward meeting the objective or the plans which they announced so boldly in the press and otherwise two years ago.
Secondly, I said that the bill provides only partial justice to the aged. Twenty years ago the pension was $20 a month; four years ago it was raised to $25 a month.

Now it is to be raised to $30 a month. I pointed out the increase in the cost of living, the increase in industrial wages, the increase in the incomes of everybody else. These old people now get only $60 a year increase from this government. I said this was a complete reversal of government policy. Two years ago they promised old age pensions at seventy without the means test. I want to read their promises of that time, found in this document "Proposals of the Government of Canada". Here is what they have to say on national old age pensions at age seventy, on page 37:
As part of the general proposals now put before the conference, it is proposed that the federal government would establish a system of national old age pensions entirely financed and administered by the federal government, and paid at the uniform rate of $30 per month regardless of means to men and women aged seventy and over in all parts of Canada.
As I said before, the present bill does not carry out either of those promises. Then it goes on:
The cost of national old age pensions by ,1948, for example, is estimated at $200,000,000.
Now the government brings in a watered-down proposal which, according to the minister himself, will cost them no more than $20,000,000 and probably less. Our estimate is considerably less.

It goes on:
There would be a partial recovery- from people over seventy paying income tax.
Then they enlarge upon these promises in this way:
The principal feature of the proposed national old age pensions is the elimination of the means test after reaching agt seventy,-
But it is not eliminated in this bill.
-regarding this (the means test) as unsuitable for the oldest group in the community over eighty per cent of whom are not in fact capable of supporting themselves in useful remunerative work. Payment of pensions as of right to people of this age offers the best kind of economic security.
Yet they do not do it in the bill they bring in. I read on:
It removes the fear of destitution much more certainly than any other method, and relieves old people of the necessity of seeking work, or of endeavouring to keep on working in unfavourable circumstances and beyond the age at which they should be able to retire, without dependence on charity or burdening the family.
These are all arguments for a great programme; then they come along with this mild edition of it and ask us to accept it.
In addition to providing a minimum subsistence for those with no other resources, this system would enable other persons with moderate private savings to retire from active work sooner, or in more comfort, than would otherwise be possible.
Then they go on:
The removal of the means test would make it possible for these pensions to be administered by the federal government alone on a uniform national basis, without the necessity for provincial participation, and would therefore considerably relieve provincial finances.
Yet they do not remove the means test.
As the federal government would be assuming full financial responsibility, it would also administer the payment of these pensions.
So much for these particular promises of two years ago and the government's promise to carry it out. No wonder the minister devotes two-thirds of his speech to excusing himself for not carrying it out.
Then I said the government had completely reversed its policy in another way. It promised an old age assistance plan for persons between sixty-five and sixty-nine years of age, the cost to be borne equally by the dominion and the provinces. Here is what they had to say on that point at that time. I am reading from page 38 of the government's document. These are the words of the government:
In addition, it is proposed to provide old age assistance for persons of age sixty-five-sixty-nine, in eases of need and in accordance with local conditions and individual circumstances, under dominion-provincial agreements broadly similar to those presently existing with respect to old age pensions for persons of age seventy and over, but with certain changes designed to liberalize the conditions under which assistance is given.
Those are the promises to persons between sixty-five and sixty-nine years of age, but there is nothing at all in this proposed measure

The proposal is that the provincial governments should administer this old age assistance and that the federal government should contribute fifty per cent of the cost, up to fifty per cent of $30 per month. The total cost of this measure by 1948 is estimated at $34 to $40 million . . .
This one feature of their 1945 proposals they say would cost from $34 to $40 million; now the minister himself estimates that the whole additional cost of all the government is proposing will be only $20 million.

Then in elaborating this particular feature of the policy which they have now discarded they go on to say:
The minimum age for national old age pensions must be definite and fixed; it cannot vary with individual cases. It must be recognized, however, that there will be an intermediate age group in which a significant minority of persons will be unable, by reason of age, to support themselves without assistance. These persons who, in fact, suffer from the disability which old age pensions are intended to assist, should not be left with no other resources than local poor relief for the temporary period which must elapse till they reach the qualifying age for old age pensions.
Yet they bring forward a measure that contains nothing for these people between sixty-five andl sixty-nine years of age.
Accordingly, it is proposed that the existing system of joint dominion-provincial old age assistance on a means test basis, which it is proposed to supersede as regards persons of seventy and over, should be adapted to meet the needs in particular cases of persons of age sixty-five-sixty-nine, with a federal government contribution of fifty per cent of the cost.
Those are the three main features of the much-heralded policy of the government of two years ago, which I believe most people in this country thought was a good plan. And this bill is the watered-down sample brought forward today by the minister. It carries out none of these promises. My fourth criticism is that the government plan offers no consideration for blind persons under forty years of age. A few years ago an amendment was brought in to the old age pensions legislation providing for pensions to blind persons; but it was stipulated that no blind person under forty years of age could benefit by the provisions of that legislation. Now the government comes along and proposes certain additions to the pensions for blind persons over

forty years of age, but does nothing at all for those under that age. I suggest this is a serious criticism of this measure.
The question of cost has been referred to. The minister has told us what it is estimated this plan will cost, and has given some other figures. I took the trouble to have some figures of an historical character looked up in connection with this measure. This legislation was passed in 1927. It did not get going fully for several years. The first year it only cost this country $131,000. In 1931-32 it cost approximately $10,000,000, in round figures. In 1941^12 the cost was $28,000,000. Under the present act it will be about $65,000,000.

It is estimated that pensions for people seventy years of age and over, with no means test, at $30 a month, would cost $200,000,000 a year. It is estimated also that pensions at sixty-five and over, at $30 a month with no means test, would cost about $336,000,000 a year; and it is further estimated that a plan covering people sixty-five years of age and over, at $50 a month with no means test, would cost this nation $560,000,000 a year. That is the material side of this question, which of course is important, just as it is important to recognize that the aged poor must have from some source, this government or the governments combined, enough to meet their needs on a cost of living basis, regardless of all other conditions.
I have here some details in connection with the supplemental allowances granted by the various provinces for old age pensions. That might be put on the record at a later stage, when we are in committee. It indicates that the different provinces have proceeded along somewhat different lines. Some have been more generous than others. But perhaps it might be well to put this information on record now; I can do so in three or four minutes and then it will be there for the information of hon. members.
Manitoba, British Columbia, Alberta and Nova Scotia made provision for the payment of supplemental allowances to old age pensioners before the passing of the dominion order in council, P.C. 6367, dated August 10, 1943, which authorized a supplement of not over $5 a month to be paid by the dominion and the provinces on the same basis as the pensions, 75 per cent and 25 per cent respectively.
Alberta was one of the first to move in this direction. In 1942 they authorized an addi-

tional allowance of So a month from January 1, 1942, and authorized an agreement with the dominion government relating to supplementary allowances. That is still being paid.
British Columbia made its increase effective on April 1, 1942. It authorized a cost of living bonus of $5 a month. This was raised to $10 on January 1, 1947. No part of the bonus is recoverable from the dominion, and it is being paid in addition to the dominion government increase granted in August, 1943.
I do not suppose the minister has any intimation from any of these provinces as to what their attitude will be with respect to *	- supplementary aids, when this new

In 1943 Manitoba made provision for a supplementary allowance of $125 a month, which it recognized as its share of a possible contribution of $5 a month by the dominion. This is still being paid.
Nova Scotia commenced its supplementary assistance in April of 1943. It provides for a supplementary allowance not exceeding $10 a month. It could allow up to that much, if the income exclusive of pension is $125 a year or less. But the allowance with the pensioner's income is not to exceed $365 a year. No such allowance was to be paid for any period before June 1, 1943. This allowance is still being paid.

First, it comes in too late. The government is too late in bringing it forward.
