-and that on matters pertaining to industrial and social legislation an effort should be made to overcome any question of jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces by effective cooperation between the several governments-
And so on. What I have read was adopted in the city of Ottawa as part of the Liberal platform in the year 1919, twenty-eight years ago. I ask you, Mr. Speaker and hon. members of the house, to look it over and see how many of those promises have been fulfilled in the course of twenty-eight years.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: You have a manifesto issued at Regina.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Certainly, but we have never been in office. Let me say this to my hon. friend, that one C.C.F. government that was elected to office in a province in its first two years in office put into effect every promise it made to the electors of that province. Laugh that off. That was done not in twenty-eight years but in two years. This afternoon what have we got?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Saskatchewan does not pay as high an old age pension as British Columbia, if you want to talk about what Saskatchewan is doing.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
To begin with, the
federal government recognizes that Saskatchewan has not the resources of British Columbia. That was recognized in the grants made to Saskatchewan through the dominion-provincial tax agreement. Moreover if Saskatchewan is not paying as high an old age pension as British Columbia, the government of Saskatchewan on slender resources has done something which is even more appreciated by the old age pensioners of that province, and that was to give them free medical, dental, optical

Old Age Pensions
and other services for the last two years. Count that up in dollars and cents and see what it is worth.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: And how much are the people taxed there?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I am not discussing
British Columbia, I am not discussing Ontario, and I am not answering the foolish and revealing question just interjected by my hon. friend of the Progressive Conservative Party. I am very glad to have the support of hon. gentlemen to my right this afternoon, but I know their record in regard to old age pensions. It was the Conservative party in the old days which did its level best through its friends in another place to block the introduction of old age pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: They did block it.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I remember that. We have heard a great deal from my hon. friends to my right in the last few months about the necessity of cutting the estimates by one-third. If you do that, you cannot grant mcreases to the old age pensioners in this country.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Oh, yes; you can.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
My hon. friend says, you can. I challenge my hon. friend to come before the house and say where he will cut the estimates to that extent. Let him give us a clear indication of where he would save the money.
What I rose to say this afternoon was this. The view of the party I have the honour to lead in this house at the moment is well known to every hon. member, and it is pretty well known throughout the country. I say with a good deal of pride that my predecessor in this seat, the late J. S. Woodsworth, toiled unremittingly to establish in this country a system of old age pensions and social security. I want to tell my hon. friends on both sides of the house that one of the most cherished possessions we have hanging framed on the wall in our national office is an exchange of letters between the late leader of this movement, Mr. Woodsworth, and the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) in that fateful year, 1926, when neither Mr. Meighen nor the present Prime Minister commanded a majority in this house but were dependent upon the votes of Mr. Woodsworth and his labour colleagues. A letter was written to both hon. gentlemen. Mr. Meighen promised that he would consider the introduction of old age pensions and of unemployment insurance if he were accorded support on a vote of confidence motion. Mr. King said that if he were accorded that support he would
introduce old age pensions at that session and would consider unemployment insurance. Mr. Woodsworth supported the vote of confidence in the present Prime Minister of Canada, and that is how old age pensions came to Canada. I am glad to pay that tribute to the late Mr. Woodsworth. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) knows perfectly well that when he ran as a labour candidate in the city of Hamilton and was elected to this parliament, before he jumped the fence-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: As you did too.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: No, that is wrong, but let me put it this way: before he fell over the fence when straddling it my hon. friend was largely elected on the statement that Mr. J. S. Woodsworth and the Labour party had secured old age pensions in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would give some credit to the trades union movement in this country and to many of us who came to see the Prime Minister of Canada.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I will give credit where it is due. Mr. Woodsworth was not alone. No one man in this country could have achieved it alone. I am pleased to pay tribute to the labour movement in this country which first nominated and elected Mr. Woodsworth to this parliament. I think it is a tribute I should pay.
It is now twenty years since the present government introduced some measure of retiring allowance for-I am not going to refer to them as the aged poor; let me call them the senior citizens of this country, those who have performed a service to Canada over the major portions of their working lives. Once more across this country we have heard the swelling of the voices demanding a greater measure of justice for these people. A short time ago I had the honour and privilege of presenting to this house a petition signed by over 250,000 citizens, and may I say that not very much effort was required in putting the petition before the people across this country. Signatures were easy to get for it, because the people of Canada want a squarer deal for senior citizens. I do not think there is a member of this house who has not been receiving in his mail almost every day letters pointing out the necessity of improving conditions for the aged; and may I add, that many of the persons who signed the petition and sent in letters are to my personal knowledge not themselves in dire need. The people of Canada, men and women of all ages, have come to recognize that the treatment of our
Old Age Pensions

old folk in Canada is entirely inadequate. They recognize that no mere five dollar increase such as is proposed in this bill, of which the federal government pays 75 per cent of the cost, is sufficient to alleviate the conditions under which those who are dependent upon the old age pension are now suffering. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) indicated, no group in this country has been harder hit by increased prices and by the removal of price controls than the aged people about whom we are talking this afternoon, those who are trying to get along on some sort of pension, and others who are attempting to live on a small fixed income. Parliament at this session decided to allow the cost of living to rise. Consequently many of the disabilities from which the older citizens suffer today are due to the action of this parliament in permitting an increase in the cost of living through the removal of beneficial controls. Now we say that the aged- and this bill covers only those of seventy- and the blind-and, as the leader of the opposition pointed out a few moments ago they are covered only if they are over forty-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Forty and over.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
If they are forty and
over. We say that the aged and the blind require at least fifty dollars a month in order to maintain anything like a little home and receive some comfort in it. I have no doubt that in this debate we shall have this bill compared with old age pensions of other countries. The minister nods his head.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
What I meant by that
nod was that this country compares most favourably with any other country in the matter of social security.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I shall deal with that
in a moment. And it will be said-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: It will be said fairly.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
-that there are no
countries with pensions as high as $50 a month. Well, in some of the Scandinavian countries they are going up toward that figure pretty rapidly; but I should like to point out in that regard that you cannot make comparisons without comparing the cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
It may be said that
in New Zealand, for example, those who get old age benefits and universal superannuation will receive only about $35 a month. But in this connection I draw the minister's attention to the fact that it is possible to rent a decent house in New Zealand for $18 a month.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Subsidized.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Of course it is subsidized. I know it is subsidized, but whether subsidized or not it is possible for an aged couple to get a decent house at $18 a month. Where can you get a decent house in Canada at that rate?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Where you subsidize
millionaires.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, and insurance
companies to build houses. I am certain that you cannot do it under the policy which was enunciated in the house by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) a short time ago, that four or five-roomed units were to be built to rent at from $50 to $70 a month, not more than $70 a month.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Is it not the fairest way to ask how much labour a man puts in to purchase these things?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, that is true, but
let me point out to the hon. member that the minister is comparing money values.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
The minister said that
they did not have as much as $50 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt
the hon. gentleman, but when I come to comparisons I shall show that, after taking into account the cost of living in Canada, the system of old age pensions envisaged by this bill will compare favourably with that of any other country in the world.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
We shall wait until
the minister does that. In the meantime I am going to have my say on the same point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
And no one will listen
with greater pleasure than I.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I dispute the point.
I go to Britain where there has been a substantial increase in the old age pension. While it looks very little in pounds, shillings and pence, I hold in my hand something I clipped from the Montreal Gazette of today just as I was coming down to the house. It is an article written by a gentleman whom I do not know, but I imagine the minister knows him because his name is Richard Graybiel of the Windsor Star.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: An excellent journalist and a good friend.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
The article reads as follows:
Goodbye, England. You have been a good host to us during the last eight months, and we are really sorry to be leaving.

Old Age Pensions
We've done a great deal of grousing about conditions here, probably haven't praised you enough for your achievements. Our basic food items-bread, milk, fats, meat, potatoes-cost less than they would almost anywhere else in the world. We marvel at the modern apartments you have built on the site of sprawling slums, apartments where a working man can house his family for two or three dollars a week.
I just put that before the house to indicate that a dollar in some countries will buy a good deal more than it will buy in our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I say at once that that is absolutely inaccurate.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I must contradict the minister flatly. I know better. I can take my hon. friend to any of the large cities, Sheffield, Birmingham and the suburbs of London and I can show him the kind of houses that can be rented for that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I know them all.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Yes, the minister knows them. Why contradict me?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Because I think it is wrong. I think the prices there are wrong.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Therefore I say that you cannot compare dollars and cents between two countries. Of course there they have now a social security system which gives them a measure of security from the cradle to the grave. A little known fact in this country is that the necessities of life and rent have been pinned down rigidly in Britain and, as I have been told by members of parliament who are not of the party in power, that the stories of starvation in Britain are wrong; that the working man and the little child are today better fed than they were before the war, because of rationing and that the present government has had the moral courage to maintain controls and rationing and so on to ensure that that shall be so. That is true. My hon. friend shakes his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt again; it is impolite. I have met several people from the old country in the last two or three weeks and my information is entirely contrary to what my hon. friend has said.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should take lessons in diction from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I ask the hon. member for Temiscouata not to be a pot-bellied valiant.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should be very grateful if these pleasant exchanges
between the minister and the hon. member for Temiscouata were kept out of my speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: May I tender my apologies to my hon. friend.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
What I was going to add was this, in spite of the devastation of war, in the British isles they have been able to improve the conditions of the old age pensioner, while we, suffering from no devastation and no destruction from war, with a functioning economy and prosperity such as we have seldom if ever known, are able to do only what is being done this afternoon.
We have always said that the amount of the old age pension should be based upon the national income of our country, bearing in mind its total population, and that it should be considered in relation to the per capita income of our own people. Our national income has doubled during the war while our population has changed relatively little, so that our per capita income must be high. During the war a very large proportion of our production went into the war effort. I was interested this afternoon in hearing the minister give the figures which he thought would be involved in the old age pension bill now before the house. He said it amounted to $65 million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: The amount is $68 million; that is the federal share. Provincial and federal will be approximately $100 million.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: We will take $100 million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Excuse me; that is for this year. It will increase every year.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend will remember that during the w*ar our national budget amounted to over $5 billion a year. In other words, the total cost of the old age pension under this bill this year, including the provinces, will be equivalent to one week's cost of the wTar. Let us put it in that light: one week's cost of the war to provide what this bill provides both federally and by the provinces for the aged of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: It is only one payment of many.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: If my hon. friend will let me make my speech, as I allowed him to make his, and reply afterward, I shall be greatly obliged.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I am very sorry.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I accept the apology. I think the house and the country will be more
Old Age Pensions

interested in getting a proper reply to the criticisms I am making now, and that reply cannot be given in these interruptions. Surely with our 750,000 or 800,000 young people back into active production, we could, if we properly planned the economy of the country, utilize our resources to produce sufficient to give our senior citizens a reasonable and decent standard of living, which we say should not be less than $50 a month.
I want to make a plea again this afternoon, as I have done before, for the complete abolition of the means test. I see no reason whatever for continuing this humiliating test, which is entirely unnecessary. In another act the government have recognized the validity of not applying the means test. They have recognized this in connection with children's allowances.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: What about New Zealand?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I am a member of parliament for Canada and I will not assume responsibility for any other country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: We hear a lot about New Zealand.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I will say to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who is muttering under his breath something which I do not quite hear, that the means test should be entirely abolished. It is humiliating, and I am pointing out that it was abolished in connection with family allowances. If it is not applied in connection with family allowances the same principle can be followed in connection with old age pensions. The fact is that many well-to-do Canadians receive family allowances and indeed were urged to apply for them, and over and above the allowance it was taxed back through income tax in proportion tc. the amount that was not needed. That is the way in which we should deal with old age pensions. If the principle is just and valid with respect to family allowances it is equally just and valid for old age pensions.
My hon. friends who believe in free enterprise are invariably telling us that we need to encourage thrift, that saving is something which is absolutely essential to the free enterprise system. I know of no greater discouragement to thrift than the means test for old age pensions. Let us take a look at it. Here is a young man, or a young woman, twenty-one or twenty-two years of age. This young man decides to take out an annuity. Suppose he goes to an insurance company or to the government. Let us say he goes to the government.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Hear, hear, says my hon. friend the member for Fort William, and I agree with him. Well, this young man takes out an annuity for $50 a month payable at the age of sixty-five. The amount he has to deposit every month-and I believe I am using the actual figure-is $8.37 or thereabouts, or approximately $100 a year. Under the scheme we have before us, when that young man, or young woman, reaches the age of sixty-five he will have denied himself at the rate of $100 a year the pleasures that some other young man or some other young woman in the same condition has enjoyed in the interval; for when they reach the age of seventy the young man and the young woman who have not denied themselves anything get the old age pension, whereas the young man or the young woman who has saved all through life at the rate of $100 a year to buy an annuity is told, "You cannot get the pension because you now have $600 a year", which in this bill is the limit of income, including pension, that anyone may receive.
That, I say, is a distinct discouragement to thrift, and I may add that in my own circle of young people, as soon as they are old enough to earn I advise them to take out a government annuity in the hope that some day the means test will be abolished and their thrift will be rewarded instead of being penalized.
I say to all my friends, particularly those who believe in free enterprise, that one thing which they should be doing is to urge, as I am doing, the abolition of the means test.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: For non-contributory pensions?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Oh, yes. I am saying this, that if a young person contributes to the purchasing for himself of a pension of $50 at the age of sixty-five or seventy he should not be penalized under this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: My question was this: Is my hon. friend advocating the abolition of the means test in connection with non-contributory pensions?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: On the same basis as judges' pensions.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Or family allowances. If I may interject this, I believe that this house would be wise to give consideration to a comprehensive social security system including old age pensions, health and all the rest of it, to which individuals would contribute during their active life. I do not know whether my hon. friend's party are on record in this regard, but we are on record-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
I just 3aid the same thing.

Old Age Pensions

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. gentleman's party is on record, but we are on record that that is a reasonable proposition, but not for a paltry $30 a month and nothing else.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Forty-eight years hence.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Yes. I have in mind a social security plan that will cover invalidity and the other hazards of life as well as old age.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
My hon.
friend spoke about not providing for the annuity because, with the means test, young people would be debarred from having the full extent of the pension. Does that not apply to every other saving as well as the saving of $100 a year for the purpose of the annuity?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Then the hon. gentleman is arguing in favour of everyone spending every cent he gets.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Oh, no. I am urging the very opposite. I am saying that the policy of the government now encourages young persons to spend every cent and not even to own a home, because if they own a home they are penalized.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Not under the regulations.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Oh, yes; $2,000 is the limit on the estate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: When we get into committee my hon. friend will see that under the new regulations that is not the case.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: I have looked at the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: When we get into committee I will show that that is not the case.

As far as the age goes, we are far behind some of the other countries. Not one of the following countries has a starting age as high as seventy:	Denmark, Sweden, France, the
United Kingdom, New Zealand, Australia and the U.S.S.R. Only one of those has a higher starting age than sixty-five and several have a lower one. It seems to me that the system in use in some countries whereby the pension is increased if the recipient is prepared to wait for a few years, is also a system which might be considered by this house, and I throw it out as a suggestion. However, that is something for the future. The point is that we are now discussing an old age pension plan to come into effect immediately, and I say that plan should be more generous and should come into effect at age sixty-five.
I agree with the leader of the opposition regarding blind pensions. I have always had a personal reason for taking a keen interest in them. I think that to set the blind pension at forty years of age is to cause hardship to large numbers of people under forty. As soon as the child! passes the period of dependency, the pension should be available. In some of our provinces that age of dependency, under the children's allowance act, is sixteen; in other provinces it is eighteen. As soon as the individual passes out of the age of dependency, the pension should be paid to the blind person.
The bill before us then is inadequate. It fails to recognize the dominion's responsibility for old age pensions. I say that the entire responsibility for old age pension payments should be in the hands of the dominion. I know that never has been the policy of my hon. friends opposite. They started with the dominion contributing fifty per cent, and when my hon. friends to my right got into office in 1930-after their leader, Mr. Bennett, had promised that the old age pension would be entirely borne by the federal authority- they raised the federal contribution to seventy-five per cent. For the reasons which I gave when I first rose to speak, I want to see the federal contribution raised to 100 per cent. Some provinces have limited resources; other provinces have greater resources. Some provinces can afford to pay something in addition while others cannot. This bill, drafted in the way in which it is drafted, does not compel any of the provinces to pay $30 a month.

That is just about the way we look at this bill. It is just about the size of

Old Age Pensions
a peanut so far as help for the aged citizens and the blind pensioners across this country is concerned. Let me say further, Mr. Speaker, that no group in this house has any monopoly on interest in the aged people. We do not pose as being the lord protectors of the aged and the blind; not by any means. I agree with what the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said in debate a short time ago, to the effect that the C.C.F. cannot lay claim to being their sole protector, nor can the Social Credit group, the Progressive Conservatives or the Liberals. In spite of the fact that the Liberal government is reputed to have introduced a bill back in 1927, I think the minister said, and that in the twenty-year period following they have brought the benefits up to the present level, I feel they must give credit to other hon. members in other parts of the house for continuously pressing for and advocating these changes, being consistent day in and day out, year in and year out in their endeavour to have these pensions improved.
There is, however, one thing I should like to say in that connection. Our movement generally, from the first year of its administration in Alberta, undertook to translate its views and philosophy into action; and, as has been stated already in this debate, in 1942 we attempted to get the dominion government to join us in increasing the pension to $30 instead of $25. The federal government could not see its way clear to do so at that time; therefore the Alberta government went it alone and paid an extra $5 per month per pensioner. That does not seem like a very large amount of money, but I would remind hon. members that with approximately 11,000 pensioners it meant a yearly outlay of over $700,000, which the Alberta government had to make by itself. That is a considerable achievement for a province the size of Alberta, with fewer than 800,000 people, particularly in the period following some devastating years through which the province had to pass. In the intervening years a programme of medical assistance has been worked out, and now Alberta is extending medical, dental and hospital facilities to the aged and blind pensioners of that province and their dependents, as well as mothers and their dependents who come under the mother's allowance there. I understand that Saskatchewan has a similar programme, and I say all honour to them for recognizing their responsibility toward the older and unfortunate citizens of this country. I merely mention these things to emphasize that at least some groups other 83166-275J
than the Liberal party have had at heart the welfare of the senior citizens and the blind in Canada.
Some things in the bill I look upon as great improvements over the old act, and I congratulate the minister on having introduced those improvements at this time. Let me say quite clearly that we do not fail to recognize that the minister is trying to operate within the restricted confines of a financial structure which perhaps makes it impossible for him to do a great deal more than he is doing at the moment. He must dip into the pockets of the taxpayers of this country to get the money he pays out in old age pensions. We realize that, and we have sympathy for him under the circumstances. I have been in a similar position, vying with other ministers in asking for money, and I know exactly what he is up against and the competition he runs into. So, as I say, while I may make some disparaging remarks about the child he has brought forth today, at the same time I have great appreciation and sympathy for him in the circumstances. It makes it very hard for our group to vote against this measure, because there are some improvements over the old act and some great benefits to our aged citizens. So I must make our position clear. We will, of course, support the minister in paying these extra benefits and in relaxing the qualifications, and what-not; but we must register our complaint that the bill falls far short of what senior Canadians had a right to expect.
For a few moments I should like to deal with the suggestion of the minister that we must have a long range programme looking toward the day when Canada can introduce a system of contributory old age pensions and social security. While the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) were speaking, I made a few hasty calculations. They may not be exactly right, but the figures will convey the general idea. I took the average head of a Canadian family. At the present rate he will have to surrender to a very much inflated state, that is to the government of Canada, $700 worth of the fruits of his labour every year in taxes. Over a period of fifty years, if this average head of a household began his active earning career at twenty years of age, he will have to surrender $35,000 to the state. When he reaches seventy years of age he has a life expectancy of eight years and 296 days, according to the latest insurance mortality tables. If at that age he becomes a pensioner and lives out his expectancy he will receive back under the

Old Age Pensions
new bill just introduced eight times $270 plus $242.50. or a total of $2,402.50, in the form of a pension.

speechtext: And will pay hidden taxes on every dollar of it.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Yes; as my hon. friend says, he will pay hidden taxes, sales and excise taxes and so on, on every single penny he spends. Let us ponder these figures for just a moment. This average head of a Canadian family is forced to surrender to the federal government-and I am speaking of the federal government only; I have neglected to calculate what he would surrender to provincial and municipal governments-$35,000 of the products of his own labour over the active years of his life. So I ask this question. Can anyone seriously or successfully argue that this average head of a Canadian family has not thereby purchased for himself social security in his old age, so long as the Canadian economy can produce sufficient goods and services to keep him in decency in his old age? I would challenge anyone successfully to argue that he has not so purchased a decent security in his old age.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext: Without contributing.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE -MODIFICATION OF ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, without contributing anything more. I maintain that he has; and I maintain, further, that all the talk about the desirability of a contributory pension in the years to come is so much eyewash. We already have a contributory shadow of a pension, and I contend that every Canadian during his active years, particularly under present circumstances with the burden of taxes he has to surrender to the state, buys a pension as of right when he is ready to retire from employment in the productive enterprise of of sixty or sixty-five. Anyone who thinks he our country, any time after he reaches the age has not should present his arguments during this debate to show that is not so.
All our tendencies in this country today are toward robbing men of their independence through taxes and death duties at rates that are punitive; and those tendencies are toward reducing the productive individual to a mere vassal of a non-productive state. As a result, many individual citizens in Canada are kept on the borderline of poverty throughout most of their lives, so that in too many cases our people simply cannot reach the age of retirement with the means to keep themselves in decency for the rest of their days. Might I suggest that if the government do not want to make pensions represent a reasonable living allowance they leave with the individual Cana-

dian over the years of his active life a greatei portion of the product of his own labour, and he will look after himself.
The Social Credit group in the house has felt since 1935, and now feels, that it will be necessary to lower the pensionable age to sixty years and to bring in a general pensions act providing for not less than $50 a month, without a means test. We have advocated that consistently.
The Alberta Social Credit government has consistently passed resolutions to induce thinking Canadians to insist that such changes be made. We do not think we should go any longer under provisions for the means test. It is unfair; it is unjust, and in future years it will become obvious that it is unworkable.
On another occasion I made our position clear by saying in effect that the absolute necessity for bringing up the pension, abolishing the means test and bringing down the pensionable age will become more apparent as the problem of unemployment develops to its full intensity, under the discredited system of finance which this government persists in following.
We are reaching the time right now when unsaleable surpluses are beginning to appear in the Canadian economy, and when provision will be made to destroy or to waste those so-called surplus products in our country. I suggest that, unless a scientific method of distributing these surpluses be found soon unemployment is bound to follow within a matter of months.
The paying of a pension of $50 to every Canadian at the age of sixty years or over may sound like a big undertaking. But in the light of the colossal gifts which Canada made to her allies during the war, and to other friends during the same period of time, and in the light of the further fact that in the giving of those colossal gifts we made ourselves more prosperous than we ever were in our lives before, the aggregate sum required to carry out the undertaking we propose becomes quite commonplace.
I know the minister is hard pressed and will continue to be hard pressed for money. He would find it difficult to implement the set of conditions we propose so long as pensions must be paid out of taxation. While that condition obtains, he will continue to have trouble. I suggest that the old age pensioners of this country, if they ever expect to receive anything like a decent standard of pensions for their maintenance in the twilight of their years, must advocate a system different from the taxation system of today. Ade-

Old Age Pensions
quate pensions will never be paid if the government has to dip into the pockets of the taxpayers to pay them.
In addition to our humanitarian interest in the welfare of our aged and blind citizens, we have other interests in this matter of old age pensions. Our interest is not in catching votes. We say that from an economic point of view it is absolutely necessary that we increase allowances to our pensioners and to the blind, if we are ever to balance consumption with production in normal times.
The minister is anxious about the selfrespect of Canada's senior citizens. That is a worthy concern. I, too, am concerned about their self-respect; and I suggest that a man's self-respect can easily be lost if he knows he is the object of charity or that what he gets by way of pension is taken from the pockets of other people. Certainly in those circumstances he loses his self-respect; I agree with that. But I say now without fear of successful contradiction that the self-respect of any man in Canada is not lost when he is placed in the position of a shareholder in Canada Unlimited -a Canada that can produce enough that every citizen can live in security during his lifetime as well as in his declining years. If he receives during those years a pension out of moneys which do not first pass through the channels of industry, more particularly will his self-respect be retained. If he sees that, while he is a shareholder in Canada Unlimited, there are being wasted hundreds of millions of dollars worth of goods and services he may be sure it is because we are proceeding under an outdated and outmoded financial system which will not distribute those goods and services.

Perfectly true. It is high time we began to recognize the need for saving what is otherwise wasted. When we do save, let us see that it is not wasted. The first thought that comes to the mind of any Social Creditor-indeed, to the mind of any decent Canadian-is: let us use the millions of dollars worth of goods and services in normal times wasted to improve the lot of the unfortunate citizens of this country, including the aged and the blind.
I wish to say just a word with respect to one other feature of the bill. After it has been passed, and while the minister is carrying on what I think should be conferences with the provinces, I hope he will have in mind the possibility of simplifying the administration of old age pensions. I had something to do with their administration for a period of eight years in Alberta, and I know the many difficulties of administering pensions under a divided authority and under the regulations as they have existed.

Let us say that they reach that age after living in Canada for eight or ten, or perhaps even only five or six years. At the present time I understand- that there is no reciprocal arrangements between Britain and Canada, with the result that many Britishers who have reached the age of seventy years while in Canada and find themselves without the means of sustenance, are not able to obtain pensions. If I am wrong I should like to be corrected. Perhaps in his rebuttal the minister will make that point clear.
In conclusion, let me, say that certainly we will support what the minister has brought forward; but we deplore the fact that the pensions paid to the aged people of Canada have not in any way increased with the cost of living in this country. We deplore the conditions under which many of our citizens have had to live during past years. We will continue to press with all our might for a sane and Christian system of pensions which at, let us say, the age of sixty or sixty-five, will provide to

every Canadian a reasonable amount on which he or she can live in happiness during declining years. Let that pension be as a matter of right. That is our position.

There are two other matters on which something needs to be said. I am not going to deal with the administrative part of the bill. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) indicated that there might be administrative difficulties. There are administrative difficulties, and they are not easy to hurdle. Steps should be taken to lay down a uniform administration of some kind and to simplify the administration. Today we have local boards. We are the only province
Old Age Pensions

in Canada which still maintains these cumbersome local boards whereby the old age pensioner in a small town has to pass through various hands. Rather than face up to it, many of them go without pensions far longer than they ought to. These are administrative matters that are of some consequence.
There are two things in this bill that particularly appeal to me. One is the matter of clarification of residence and the other that of nationality. They did not attract a great deal of attention when the matter was discussed, except for a few words here and there, but they are important. A large minority of Canadians will rejoice over the liberal wording of these two clauses in the resolution. At times every hon. member has had instances of persons come to his attention who were born in Canada and who lived here almost all their lives. Because they went away from Canada for five or ten years in the period between their fiftieth and seventieth years they found on their return to their native country, that they could not qualify for old age pensions. I am thinking now of a specific case_ of a man who was born in Canada and lived here until 1916. He went to the United States and was absent from 1916 to 1935. At seventy years of age he applied for the old age pension. This man had lived in Canada fifty-one years but had lived here only twelve years out of the last twenty. At that time he was advised that he was not eligible for the old age pension. This bill now corrects what I thought was a mistake and what is now recognized to be a mistake.
The bill is also more generous with respect to those who are now in Canada but who are not citizens of Canada. There are a great number of people who were born in other lands and who, for some reason or another had not become naturalized. They have spent the required number of years in this country. They have contributed to the general economy even though they were not citizens. They have paid their taxes; they have worked in our factories and on our farms; but, for one reason or another, perhaps because they came too late in life to learn the English or the French language, or perhaps for some other reason, perhaps just from neglect, they have not become naturalized. It is to the credit of this government that they have decided to follow the precedent established in the unemployment insurance and the family allowance measures and extend the benefits of old age pensions to all persons in this country

over seventy years of age who have completed the required period of residence or otherwise complied with the act.
I said a few moments ago that this debate would be an acceptance of what we have offered to do, but that we would immediately begin a new fight for improvements. In the field of social service we can never stand still. The status quo is never good enough. We must continue constantly to go forward and we must do a thorough job of it. I appreciate that putting a few blow-out patches on the 1927 act, now twenty years old, is just a beginning. We are now living in an age that calls for a new social deal, not only for the underprivileged, but for the aged and the needy.
It must be said in fairness that this bill is a step forward, but it only touches the fringes of the problem. In an appreciation of the problem of old. age pensions there are three considerations which are uppermost in our minds and which have been touched on by speakers who have already taken part in the debate. These are the means test, the amount of pension, and the age at which pensions become payable.
I should like to consider these for a few moments. Two years ago I described the means test by referring to it as invidious or, as I believe a member of the house referred to it, as the poverty test. I have not changed my mind on that. It is a hangover from the old days of the poor laws when a person claiming a pension had to prove himself completely destitute and without relatives to support him. I know it is beyond question that a great number of deserving people are debarred from receiving a pension because they cannot submit themselves to the indignity of the means test; yet we are forced to insist upon it and, by doing so, we condemn some of them to an old age that is barren and cheerless poverty. This bill is an improvement. A person may have an income of $600 a year. It is a tremendous improvement over the previous limit of $425, but I, too, say that it is not enough. It seems to me that we are setting a maximum living standard of $600 a year for our senior citizens, and I would ask this question: Are we justified in requiring old persons to live on a maximum of $600 a year when we consider that the benefits of unem-ploj'tnent insurance, inadequate as they are, assure to a single person without dependents, who has been earning $26 a week, a maximum of $636 for a year? A man of seventy years of age has basically the same needs for food1.

Old Age Pensions
clothing and recreation as the man who is younger and he must pay the same prices.
I have always been opposed to the means test. It is archaic and ungenerous. I wonder if we in Canada cannot afford the dignity of an old age pension free from that test. I could not agree with the leader of the opposition when he said that we had reneged on our promises made in this house two years ago in the white paper. I have here the statement made today by the minister in which he recalls the proposals made in August, 1945, to the provinces with respect to a programme for national health, public investment and social security, and he reiterates that we stand by them now as we stood by them at that time. That certainly envisaged a contributory old age pension scheme.
May I touch upon another matter. I wish it were not necessary to shame ourselves into taking some of these forward steps in social services. I am a little bit tired, as I know other members are, of pointing out what other governments are achieving in progressive little countries like New Zealand, Denmark and Sweden, and then calling upon this great country of ours to catch up with them. In every branch of social welfare, from old age pensions, yes, to divorce, we have always had to wait for someone else to show us the way. Why can we not show these other countries an example of humane and advanced social legislation?
I said a few minutes ago that we did envisage such a plan in 1945. In so far as the basic pension is concerned, it will be of little value to specify an optimum amount of pension that should be paid. Clearly $28 a month paid in Ontario is not enough. Previous speakers have suggested $50 a month as adequate. I should like to have voted for $50 a month. I believe it would far more nearly meet the situation. But personally I think it is a very poor idea for the various political parties to start bidding against one another in this matter. For my own part I should like to see the old age pension raised to the highest possible level, but rather than name an arbitrary figure I think the government should relate the old age pension directly to the cost of living as it fluctuates from time to time.

Such a supplement would rise or fall with the cost of living index, always leaving the basic rate unchanged, which is now $30.
Finally, there was a question of the qualifying age, the age at which the pension should be payable. In different countries opinions vary on this point and they change with the economic cycle. In bad times there is a tendency to lower the pension age and to tempt the needy people out of the labour market and so make room for younger workers. While it is true that in an expanding economy like ours there is room for every employable person, I consider it wrong for us to compel senior citizens to work by setting the qualifying age so high. As a guiding principle we ought, to adopt the recommendation of the 1932 international labour conference, that the pensionable age be set at not more than sixty-five, and in doing so we would only be following the example set by almost every other civilized country in the world, as was pointed out by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell). In at least nine countries-the United States, England, New Zealand, France, Australia, Czechoslovakia, Sweden, Denmark and the Soviet Union-the pensionable age has been fixed at sixty-five or less.

Among the great middle

speechtext:
There is another matter which I think ought to be given consideration. There is a situation which frequently arises-and it was referred to on the floor of the house, I think by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley)-where the head of the house is unable to work and draws the old age

Old Age Pensions

pension. His wife is younger than he is, but not eligible under the statute. Both of them must try to live on his pension. I think it is high time, in cases where the wife is unable to work, that the regulations be changed so that the pension to her becomes automatic. That may appear to be a small point, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the lack of just such a simple provision is causing real hardship in many families throughout this country.
These many things about which I have been talking-abolition of the means test, increase in the amount of pension, lowering of the qualifying age-cover only half the problem. Taking care of Canada's senior citizens is more than a matter of dollars and cents. Even though they have withdrawn from active participation in business and industry, we cannot feel that they are not members of the community and that they have not a place in society. They are not to be just pensioned off and forgotten. This is becoming a really serious social problem in view of the changing position of Canada. We have always looked upon ourselves as a young country. The emphasis has always been on youth. Yet it is calculated that, within a generation and a half, thirty per cent of Canada's population will be over fifty-five years of age. This inevitable trend toward an older population is a matter of some significance. I have here a newspaper report, from the New York Times, of a statement made last month by the director of the social science department of the university of Michigan. This is what he said in part:
For one thing the political power of the older person will grow. With that development will come more and more demands for social security. Old age insurance will become more important. Business will be giving more attention to annuity and pension plans. Taxes for support of old age persons will rise sharply. Positions of importance in government and business are more apt to be held by older persons.
Consumer demands also will change. Our recreation planning will have to take into account the demands of older persons. Travel should increase and books and concerts should become more popular. Population shifts will continue as the older people, who have retired, drift to the states with the mild winter climates.
These are just a few of the changes which we may expect to find mirrored in our own society in the next twenty-five years, and we must begin to plan now to cope with them. We must prepare to face the growing problems of support, physical and mental health, recreation and social relations, of our senior citizens who, within the next thirty years, will comprise at least one-third of our population. In the post-war world we are trying to fit everyone
[Mr. Croll.l
into a spot. We have not yet successfully fitted our older generation in at all. Unless we do something more than we have done up to the present time, we shall build up a Townsend movement for social security which will crusade with more zeal than good sense. If we can ensure for all Canadians a broad programme of social services, we are not likely to be troubled with fabulous plans for $200 or $300 a month pensions and the like.
But money payments are not the whole answer. Britain and other countries supplement the cash pension, not only with medical services, but with extra food, recreation, health services, and even domestic aids for pensioners. In my own province of Ontario we not only pay low pensions but provide none of those social services. It is the duty of the government and the community to do more than they are doing at the present time. They must provide community centres, clubrooms and other facilities for the use of the old people. Perhaps some of our existing facilities might be reserved exclusively on specific days for these older people, as is done in the United States and Britain. The older third of the nation made Canada what it is today; and to them we still look for counsel and example. We must neither forget them nor take them for granted. As members of parliament charged with responsibility, we must do everything in our power, not only to make their lives richer, but to make them more meaningful.

To those not acquainted with the situation in this province, his remarks today must have left the impression that Ontario was lagging behind, whereas Ontario has been the pioneer and, under the present government of that province, still holds the leadership.
Neither were we told by the minister or by the hon. member of Spadina that it was a Conservative government under Mr. Bennett that in 1931, on behalf of the dominion, recognized and assumed the dominion's primary obligation with respect to old age pensions. I lay at the door of this government responsibility for the fact that none of the provinces, with the exception of British Columbia, have been taking steps in

this field in recent months. Why should they, when the air was filled with uncertainty because of the vaporizing of this government?
While I am on that subject, may I remind hon. members that the premier of British Columbia has been asking this government to call a conference so that this whole question may be the subject of sensible negotiation. The dominion government still refuse to call that conference; apparently they do not want negotiation. The premier of British Columbia also made it clear that he hoped the increase introduced at the recent session of the British Columbia legislature would not be required for more than a temporary period, because it was his hope that this government would rise to its responsibilities and not seek to cast the burden on the provinces. Here is a Canadian press dispatch under date of February 11, reporting on the joint announcement of that day by Premier John Hart, finance minister Herbert Anscomb and provincial secretary George S. Pearson, with regard to the increase in the old age pension in that province, at the entire expense of the province. The dispatch states:
Old age pensioners in British Columbia will receive a '$5 cost of living bonus retroactive to January 1 this year, a joint announcement by Premier John Hart, finance minister Herbert Anscomb and provincial secretary George S. Pearson said today.
May I just pause there to say that British Columbia had the courage to make the increase in old age pensions retroactive to January 1. The best this government can do under the present measure is to start it from May 1. The dispatch continues:
The bonus, second to be granted by the province, will bring the monthly old age allowance to $35. Of this amount British Columbia will pay $16.25 and the federal government $18.75.
Premier Hart said the bonus was being given for a temporary period pending revision of the old age pension arrangements by the dominion government.
Let us bear that well in mind. Let the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who comes from that province, bear that in mind when he gives some indication of support for the proposals advanced today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and when he takes great credit-as credit is due-to the government of British Columbia for doing what the delays of this government compelled that province to do.
I shall read that again:
Premier Hart said the bonus was being given for a temporary period pending revision of the old-age pension arrangements by the dominion government.
The premier said that, while in Ottawa last November, he was assured by Prime Minister King that the moment a sufficient number of

Old Age Pensions
provinces had signed agreements, he would call a conference to discuss the question of implementing the social security measures and public investment programme submitted to the dominion-provincial conference in August, 1945.
I interject there that they have seven provinces now, but they are no nearer to calling a conference. The government always has some excuse for not calling a conference together, when everyone knows it ought to be called.
The dispatch continues:
"It now is my intention to press for a convening of that conference and I have every hope that more generous treatment will be accorded those in receipt of old age pensions," Mr. Hart said.
The new bonus will cost the province $900,000 annually. Total amount now paid out in pensions to British Columbia's 18,000 pensioners is $5,700,000 annually, of which the dominion's share is $3,761,000.
It is perfectly clear from the statement made by Premier John Hart that he expected the dominion would rise to its responsibilities. He demanded or requested that the dominion government should measure up to its responsibilities, and call a conference to work out a new agreement. But it is clear that the government of British Columbia was not recognizing any obligation on the province to assume the primary load or the primary responsibility in respect of old age pensions. That responsibility, in his statement, rests with the dominion government.
If that responsibility is not to be discharged, if the dominion government is simply going to fold its hands in the face of the need, and say to the provinces, "Well, thus far we will go, and no farther; if pensioners do not get enough, from that point on it will be your responsibility"-
