SB. To reclaim and to prevent the flooding of valuable agricultural lands in the valley of the Lillooet river, near Pemberton, B.C., $100,000.

I was asking some questions on this item when the house rose last night. I want to make it clear that we from British Columbia are not objecting to this money being spent there, but should like to know whether the provincial government and the farmers concerned are putting up any money? How is it that this particular project was given preference? If the minister would give an explanation the item might pass.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The item is to cover a project which has been under way for some time. It was undertaken, in the first place, by P.F.R.A., but not as a P.F.R.A. project. People of that area made representations to the government to the effect that a number of returned soldiers had been settled in that area by the federal government and that each year the area was flooded just about the time the returned men were ready to put in their crops. The land was flooded as a result of waters coming down from the glacier which feeds the stream. About seeding time the floods were at their height and it became almost impossible for these men to make a living on this land. I had the privilege of visiting that area myself some years ago, I think in 1938. I looked over it, and anyone knowing the circumstances that exist there should be able to see that people cannot make a living on that land unless something is done. Personally I think that when a government, be it federal, provincial or municipal, puts a number of human beings on a piece of land I am satisfied that it has assumed a responsibility towards those settlers and that it should attempt to rectify the circumstances which prevent such men from making a living.
It is one of the most beautiful valleys that can be found anywhere in the dominion, and the land these men are on can be made the finest farm land in Canada. I cannot imagine any finer homes anywhere in the world than

Supply-Agriculture
can be established in this valley. These men are in there-I have forgotten the exact number of them, but I could get that information if requiredr-and they have built nice little homes. Most of them have put up bams, and then they found that all that was needed to destroy their work for the whole season was for a few trees or some other obstruction to fall into the stream to cause it to overflow and flood their land. Because of the river being held back to a level which came up almost to the level of the land, a slight blockade would cause the river to overflow and flood their land. After having seen this actually happen at a season of the year when the land was being flooded, and believing that I knew something of the possibilities of that area, I asked the government to provide $10,000 to have an investigation made as to what might be done purely as an experimental project to ascertain what could be done, in British Columbia in spots of that kind, and more particularly to give some service to these returned men who, some years ago after the end of the first war, had been placed in that area.
We had an investigation made and our engineers examined the whole project and made a report. I have a summary of their report before me, and I do not think the remarks that were made last evening should be allowed to stand as made without some correction, because they give a different impression from the facts as we know them.
The area is divided into three different projects, area No. 1, area No. 2 and area No. 3. I quote now from the report:
Area No. 1
Lillooet river between Lillooet and Tenasse lakes
In considering the reclamation of area No. 1 above, being the area from Lillooet lake to Green river, the method that gives the greatest assurance of success is to lower the elevation of Lillooet lake, both at its high and low stages.
In order to lower the level of Lillooet lake, both at low water and at high water, we proposed to construct a channel 300 feet wide at the bottom with side slopes of two to one over its entire length of 6,000 feet.
The report goes on to deal with the estimated cost per acre of the reclaimed land in this area, and says:
The cost per acre of land which will foe reclaimed directly due to the lowering of the lake will foe $131.50 per acre.
I think that was the figure mentioned by my hon. friend last night as the cost per acre of the project. It goes on:
This land at the moment is not being used for agricultural purposes, nor can it in its present state so be used. This is the cost when the total estimated cost has been charged to the land directly benefited. However, the effect of this lowering of the lake will be felt far beyond this
area, as the success of the proposed works farther above in area No. 2 will depend in considerable degree on the lowering of the high water in Lillooet river at the mouth of Green river. Thus a certain proportion of this cost should be charged against lands in area No. 2.
In any event the reclamation of 2,706 acres of land at a price of $131.50 per acre appears to us to be worth while. The amount of such arable land in British Columbia is limited, and only occurs in our valleys. The benefits of this productivity to the district as well as to the province are quite apparent.
Area No. 2
Area No. 2 comprises all the land lying south and west of the Lillooet river, lying between Green river on the south and Miller creek on the north. The success of the reclamation of this area depends in a large measure on the degree of scouring of the bottom of the Lillooet river below Green river clue to the lowering of the high water level of Lillooet lake. This scouring will have to be assisted where submerged logs or snags occur.
Cost per acre: The cost per acre of the works is $27.96. The benefits derived should soon pay the cost. Total cost of this project would be $55,915.
We are confident that the work outlined for area No. 2 will ensure reasonable reclamation.
Area No. 3
Area No. 3 comprises all the land west of the Lillooet river lying north of Miller creek and south of the north fork of Ryan creek. This area includes the district called Pemberton Meadows and is the most thickly settled and best improved area in the valley. The land produced some of the best potatoes and turnips in the district, yields of ten and twelve tons of potatoes per acre and twenty tons of turnips being average crops. The danger of overflow from Lillooet river has al ways been present, but the good farmer usually was able to gather in his crop as only the higher ground was utilized. Ryan creek runs along the west side of the valley at a higher elevation than the most of the land. Thus we have a strip of land between the Lillooet river and Ryan creek averaging from one-half to three-quarter miles in width, in which the high ground is close to the banks of the river and the creek, and the intervening ground is three to four feet lower than the banks. Of course this is on low ground which under certain conditions becomes flooded.
Of late years the water table has risen due to seepage and overflow from Ryan creek There appears to be very little seepage from Lillooet river as its banks are composed of fine silt closely resembling clay in its appearance. Many of the farmers now find it impossible to grow potatoes on land which formerly gave good crops, and have had to use the land for grazing. This does not give nearly the returns formerly received, as there was and still is a great demand for Pemberton potatoes to be used as certified seed.
Cost per acre:	The cost per acre of the land
which will be directly benefited by these proposed works, on the basis of $62,1115.62 distributed over 2,120 acres is $29.30 per acre. We are confident that the added returns from this land will more than make up this amount.
Supply-Agriculture

Area No. 4
This comprises all the land lying north of the north fork of the Ryan creek. This area consists of land which is approximately the same height as the average high water. The grade of Lillooet river is increasing in this area. It has been frequently changing channels. Drainage ditches will help. We think that for the moment this area should not be considered. This is one of the most costly areas. We think that its treatment should be postponed until the experience gained from the river area No. 3 can be used to design the protection for this area.
All the lands in the valley are covered by the proposed agreement between the dominion, the province and the proposed Pemberton valley dyking district. Assuming that the Indian department becomes part of the Pemberton Valley dyking district-this suggestion was made last night; as our part of it is the reserve, it could be-we are informed that there is a total of 30,000 acres in the valley and covered by the agreement: 10,000 acres privately owned lands, 10,000 acres government lands and 10,000 acres Indian lands. We have no detailed break-down as to the occupancy of privately owned lands; neither have we in detail the arable acres of crown lands. The same holds for the Indian lands in the project.
There was a report made, which was known as the McGugan report, dividing the area of the Pemberton valley which will be directly benefited by the proposed works into roughly four portions, the areas of which I have just spoken. These are pretty well covered by what I have just read.
The expenditures which have been made up to date are expenditures made by the federal government. An agreement was drawn up as between the province and the association at Pemberton which has to do with the utilization of the lands afterwards and the maintenance of these lands. A copy of the agreement has just been handed to me. Since that is the question which has been asked directly, I shall deal with it from that point of view. The agreement runs as follows:
His Majesty the King in the right of Canada as represented herein by the Right Honourable James G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture for Canada, hereinafter called the Dominion
of the First Part
and
His Majesty the King in the right of the province of British Columbia as represented herein by the Honourable Edward T. Kenney, Minister of Lands and Forests for British Columbia, hereinafter called the Province
of the Second Part and
Pemberton Valley Dyking District, hereinafter called the district
of the Third Part
Whereas it is necessary and in the public interest to reclaim an area of fertile agricultural lands in the valley of the Lillooet river in the province of British Columbia and
Whereas these lands were largely settled by returned soldiers after the first world war; and
Whereas these lands are being damaged from seepage silting, stream erosion and periodic flooding from the waters of the Lillooet river and its tributaries and also great damage is being caused in the lower section of the valley by the formation of a barrier in the river between Lillooet and Tenasse lakes, which barrier raises the level of Lillooet lake and thereby causes progressive inundation of some of the best agricultural lands in the valley; and
Whereas these conditions have resulted in the almost complete abandonment of a large area of said lands by the original settlers; and
Whereas the prairie farm rehabilitation branch of the dominion Department of Agriculture has completed surveys of certain areas of the Lillooet river valley to determine what remedial works can be undertaken for the reclamation of the agricultural lands, and the rehabilitation of the settlers now resident, in the section of the Lillooet river valley above indicated; and
Whereas the surveys indicated that these lands can be reclaimed; and
Whereas the remedial measures that can be undertaken are set out in detail in a report signed by D J., McGugan, consulting engineer for the federal Department of Agriculture, dated the 10th day of August, 1945, a copy of which report is hereto attached and marked appendix "A" to this agreement;
Now, therefore, this agreement witnesseth that in consideration of the premises and the agreements hereinafter contained, each with the other, the parties hereto agree as follows:
1.	The dominion agrees forthwith with the funds appropriated by parliament in the current fiscal year and with such funds as may be appropriated for the purpose by parliament from time to time hereafter, to undertake the construction of such reclamation works as it may deem feasible and necessary to effect the reclamation of agricultural lands and the rehabilitation of settlers now resident in the section of the Lillooet river valley above indicated;
2.	The province agrees to furnish free of cost to the dominion all rights-of-way for canals, dykes, ditches, access roads, and relocation of existing roads, or such other rights-of-way as may be required for the execution of the works, provided such title thereto is now vested in and will remain in the province;
3.	The district agrees to make available free of cost to the dominion or province all rights-of-way for canals, dykes, ditches, access roads and relocation of existing roads, or such other rights-of-way as may be required for the execution of the works not provided, as above by the province.
4.	The province agrees to improve existing bridges so as to enable the dominion to transport the necessary equipment and machinery to the scene of operations and from place to place during the construction of the -work and to improve and condition such provincial roads as may be necessary to transport the necessary equipment and machinery to the scene of operations and from place to place during the construction of the works; so far as the title to said bridges and roads is now vested in the province;

Supply-Agriculture
5.	The province further agrees to obtain the release of any, and all, timber and mining leases of lands required for or in connection with the execution or construction of the works herein referred to and to make available to the dominion free of all let or hindrance the use of and access to all or any part of the lands so required;
6.	The province further agrees to make its crown lands lying in the area referred to in the premises to this agreement available for the reestablishment of returned soldiers and that, to this end it will for an indefinite period reserve such lands from other disposition;
7.	The province further agrees to cooperate with the dominion and the district and to provide any necessary legislation, and to make available its administrative machinery, to facilitate the execution of the work herein contemplated and generally to carry out the intent and spirit of this agreement;
8.	The district agrees to take over and to assume the control of the said works as soon as notified in writing by the dominion that the said works has been completed; the district further agrees that upon assuming control it will operate the said works efficiently and maintain the whole of the said works in a proper state of repair and in conformity with any statute or any statutory provisions applicable thereto, and agrees to operate and maintain the whole of the said works without expense to or assistance from the dominion;
9.	The district agrees to save, defend and keep harmless and to indemnify the dominion of, from and against all claims, charges and actions that may after the signing of this agreement be brought against the dominion by reason of anything the dominion has done or failed to do in the performance of the works undertaken pursuant to this agreement.
10.	If any question arises as to the interpretation of this agreement or whether the dominion has performed any of the things by the dominion agreed to be performed, such question shall be decided by the Minister of Agriculture for the dominion, whose decision shall be final and binding upon the parties hereto.
I think it will be agreed that the agreement makes it possible for us to go into the valley and carry on experiments in a place where we can at the same time do a great deal of good, and the results obtained from that experience can be utilized in order to set up other projects elsewhere in the province.
I would say, in answer to the suggestion contained in the question, that it is not the intention of the government to proceed with projects of this kind, with the total cost assumed by the dominion government over large areas. The intention is to use this as an experiment if we can, and utilize it for the purpose of deciding what to do elsewhere and at the same time provide relief to returned men put on the land at the end of the . first war.

I was glad to hear the minister speak in defence of this item, as, of course, one would expect him to do. I have
a considerable interest in the question myself, and on March 6, I made specific reference in this house to the Pemberton Meadows project. Hon. members will find reference to it at page 1074 of Hansard, where I mentioned that an area of several thousand acres could be brought under cultivation, an area which is considered to be one of the most fertile in the province.
As the minister has pointed out, this is designed to help settlers who have been there for many years and have done a great deal of work on the area themselves, and who now find it beyond their resources to cope with the flooding of the land without government assistance. I think it is proper for the dominion government, through the Department of Agriculture, by means of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration, and as an experiment, to go into projects of this kind, because it is not a case of throwing away money. It is not a wild-goose chase, because we know, from the fact that these have been valuable farms in the past, that whatever work may be done there will be of value to the settlers themselves, and give some indication of how this work can be carried on in the future.
The minister pointed out, I believe, that there are 30,000 acres of valuable agricultural land involved in the project, and in that connection I would refer to what the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said last night, as reported at page 4277 of Hansard. He said:
We have to go back to our people and tell them why the dominion government are going to spend nearly half a million dollars in connection with land which some of us think is not worth very much.
I would be the last to suggest that the hon. member does not know the province, because he does. He knows it thoroughly, since he has made a great study of its resources and has spent a good deal of time travelling. But he is not quite accurate in thinking that this land is not worth very much, because all reports, as verified by the minister, indicate that it is some of the finest agricultural land in the province.
I am sorry to hear any member from British Columbia discourage or criticize work that is being done by the prairie farm rehabilitation administration in that province. We have been urging for some time now that the administration should go there in a larger way than they are doing. They are undertaking only scattered surveys and we have been urging that they should go there in a larger way than contemplated in
Supply-Agriculture

this particular project on which they are working. I think we should encourage any and all work done by the administration along these lines.
There was one thing to which the minister referred that I should like to emphasize. He said that they undertook a preliminary survey, and I believe the initial outlay was some $10,000, as a result of which they were satisfied that it would be a valuable and paying project to go ahead with the work which is now being undertaken. I would repeat the request that was made last night, that they do the same thing for the whole interior of the province and make a survey. We are not asking them to rush in and spend large sums of money without investigation. We are asking that they send engineers throughout the area to make an investigation along the lines I suggested last night.
Again, with reference to this particular scheme, the hon. member for New Westminster referred to the interest of the Indian affairs branch in the question. As I understand their attitude, they are not opposed to the development, but they rather want their own lands brought under the same work which is being carried on for the white settlers. It is a question whether it will be enlarged rather than a question of their opposing any work at all.
In conclusion, I have no hesitation in supporting this particular item because it is work which will repay the capital outlay. It is work that is being done on behalf of settlers long established there who are unable to carry on without government assistance, and it is work which will enable the settlement, when this land is reclaimed, of a large number of returned soldiers of this war. I think the money involved in this item oi $100,000 is something that we should support and encourage rather than criticize.

There are one or two things that should be said for the purpose of keeping the record straight. First of all, regarding the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops, I am grateful to him for bringing to my attention what I said last night. It is true I did make the remark which he quoted, but I am frank to say that it was made after eleven o'clock and a little in haste. I did say at the time that the land was of little value. That is on record but it is somewhat of an exaggeration. I am willing to admit that tonight.
I am not objecting to this item. My principal reason in rising last evening on this item was to put my position before the committee. To my way of thinking, there is more fertile land in danger in the lower Fraser valley and elsewhere, but every time we approach the gov-
ernment we are turned down and can get no such assistance. When we see an item for $500,000 to be expended, naturally we want to know how it comes about that the dominion government can make such an expenditure and yet, when we want relief and some assistance, we are told that it is not a dominion matter, and that we have to wait until the P.F.R.A. is passed. I^e are curious to know how this item without P.F.R.A. being passed could pass the financial council of the government.
I want also to put on the record certain facts because the minister made a statement intended to correct me in regard to the figures I gave last night about the $131 an acre. I have the documents before me. There are three areas. The first will cost $355,456, which works out at $131.50 an acre. The minister rather suggested to the' committee that this $131.50 had to be spread over the three areas. Well, there is a total in the three projects of 6,826 acres and as the total expenditure is $473,785 in areas 1, 2 and 3, dividing that, the average is around $80 an acre.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The minister did not say anything. The minister read the report which my hon. friend says he has before him. The report says that.

Let us look at the report and be clear about it because I do not want the minister to get away with that and to suggest that I am quoting figures which are wrong. For area No. 1 the report gives 2,706 acres. The total expenditure is $355,756.50, and the cost per acre is $131.50. In area No. 2 the report gives the total cost as $55,913, and then at the bottom of the page gives the cost per acre as $27.96. Then we go on to area No. 3 where the total cost is given as $62,115.62, and the cost per acre as $29.30, as the minister has said. I do not know what it is going to cost per acre over the whole district, but if you take each of the areas-area No. I costing $131.50 per acre and areas No. 2 and No. 3 costing the amounts I have just quoted -and lump them altogether, as the minister,
I think, said we should have done, it works out at $80 per acre as the average. That is the record. Is it any wonder I criticize when we in the Fraser valley at the moment are faced with the loss of hundreds of farms? We are losing the fight with the Fraser river. Two or three thousand farmers do not know whether or not their farms will be washed away, the river rose so many inches today. It is different from the Ottawa river. It rises when the heat strikes the interior and the snows begin to melt. The farmers have worked hard. The last danger we had there

Supply-Agriculture
was in 1936. The fanners are taxed to the limit to keep the Fraser river within bounds. That is one of the most fertile areas in British Columbia, notwithstanding the statement made about Pemberton Meadows. Then when we are asking for relief and come here for it we are told we have to get prairie farm rehabilitation. If that is the case, how does the government come to be spending half a million dollars up in Pemberton Meadows? I leave the answer to the committee.

I hesitate to venture into a discussion on an agricultural item, but it happens that I go up through this district every summer. There is no doubt that the money voted is being well spent and there is great need there. As the Minister of Agriculture has said, the land is fertile and the settlers themselves have gone to great trouble and expense to try to solve their own problem. They have convinced both the dominion and provincial governments that something should be done. I believe the minister will agree with me that the provincial government have been in there too, have made surveys and are entirely convinced that this work should be proceeded with. I know the former member for Cariboo, who is now Hon. J. G. Turgeon, took a great interest in this work and I suppose he had a good deal to do with getting it started.
I think he did.

I do not think anything should be said in this house which would prejudice the work being carried through to a successful conclusion. We should like to support the hon. member for New Westminster in his request. I do not know, but perhaps he has been a little bit slow in making that request to the government. I know a good deal of money has been spent in his riding, in dredging and in other ways, none of which we begrudge him. But certainly it is not right that any British Columbia member should take the position that this particular vote should be cut out.
Nobody has suggested that.
It is necessary work, and I am glad the Minister of Agriculture has decided to go ahead with it. I can assure him that he will have our support.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks made by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house in regard to this item. It has to do with an area which happens to be in the southern part of the Cariboo riding and I know it very well. I want to commend the minister for the vote and to assure the committee that the work
being done there is essential and that the land is undoubtedly fertile. The government is to be commended for its efforts in this regard. I have no doubt that the hon. member for New Westminster has a legitimate protest with regard to certain parts of the country to which he has referred, but I do not think we shall get anywhere by setting one against the other. I think both these projects should be undertaken. Perhaps when the project to cope with the Fraser river which my hon. friend refers to is undertaken and when, it is worked out to so much per acre, he may find that the figure is quite as high as the figures he has just been giving the committee with respect to Pemberton Meadows. I do not wish to do any more than merely assure the committee that the work is well worth doing. Now that it has been started, I hope it will be carried through to a conclusion. In reference to the table which has been placed on the record, it will be noted that in respect of the hog marketings for Canada we reached a low point in February, 1947. as compared with the same month for 1946. The percentage of decrease was reduced to 16-2 per cent in March, and then in April it reached a point where it was approximately the same as last year. Then, in May of 1947 we have come up 8-2 per cent above the figure for 1946.
In respect of the figures for the provinces it will be noted that in Ontario we started out in January of 1947 with a small loss, and in February we had a loss of 1-2 per cent. In March, it will be noted the loss was only 0-1 per cent, and in April there was a gain of 26 per cent. Again in May the gain amounts to 32-6 per cent. So that in Ontario it is climbing fast.
However, the big improvement is seen in the figures given for Quebec. In January of this year we were up 3-8 per cent. In February it went down to the extent of 2-6 per cent, but in March it was up 20-6 per cent; in April, 41 per cent, and in May it was up 73-4 per cent. I give these figures to indicate that in our opinion the low point in the decrease in hog marketing has been passed. The figures show that during the first five months of this year Quebec has accomplished what the farmers there were asked to accomplish at the conference held last December. We asked them to produce in 1948 as many hogs as they had produced in 1945. They are now ahead of that programme. They have produced more hogs in the first five months of 1947 than they did in the first five months of 1945.
It will be noted from these figures that Ontario has accomplished the same thing. They are really a year ahead of the programme as it was set last December. Up to date our difficulty has been in the west. The figures show that in the three western provinces there was a decrease of 35-3 per cent in January, and 39-5 per cent in February. But, just as happened in the other provinces, the change came in March, when the decrease was reduced to 37-1 per cent, to 30'2 per cent in April and to 20-5 per cent in May. While our figure is still a long way below the 1915 figure, so far as the production of hogs is concerned, it will be noted that the production is on the increase. We are estimating that by August or September of this year we shall be producing in western Canada as many hogs as we produced in 1946. And we are hoping that, even in the western part of 
Canada, we shall overtake the programme set out in December and, by 1948, get our production up to the 1945 level.

I hope it is not wishful thinking on the part of the minister. As a matter of fact the statistics show that the over-all drop throughout Canada is a little more than ten per cent in respect of hog production. All hon. members know what is happening in the west. Early this spring both in the west and here in the east sows have been going to the slaughter-houses by hundreds, and the prices on little pigs have dropped by over fifty per cent in the eastern provinces in the last month. Little pigs are now being offered, and cannot be sold.
The minister thinks that by August the increase will come up to the 1946 figure. I venture to say that might take place, because so many pigs are reaching the slaughter-houses before they are ready, on account of the shortage of feed. Sows have gone, and pigs light in weight are being offered. If the minister will look into the grades he will find that within the next two months they will be light in weight. The minister considers that he will need half a million dollars more this year for grade A and B1 premiums than he needed last year. I think it will be just the other way around.

Well, that is characteristic, anyway. But we can say that the amount of bacon which has been sent to the United Kingdom has been less so far this year than it was in 1945 and 1946.
I should like to refer to the way in which our bacon is marketed in England. I understand on good authority that our bacon is

Supply-Agriculture
still being marketed there by interests who have more interest in Danish bacon than they have in Canadian bacon. If that is true-and I believe it is-it is a serious state of affairs. The minister said the other night that at the present time we are not allowed to advertise any Canadian products in England. My only comment on that is that in the main we are giving Great Britain products at a fairly good price; that is, a price reduced as compared with world prices. But if we are not given some consideration for that, then I believe the Canadian producer should have some preference over foreign producers in the English market.
I would ask the minister to make a statement with regard to the commission houses which are dealing in our Canadian bacon and selling it, and to state whether the people who have an interest in Danish bacon are also dealing in our bacon.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are no commission houses selling bacon in Great Britain at the present time. The commission houses which were doing business before the war did handle both Danish and Canadian bacon. The prices were determined by a board which sat at the beginning of each week and determined what the prices were on bacon coming from Denmark, Canada and elsewhere. But that was all discontinued during the war. There are people who say-and probably they are correct-that the same persons are making this distribution under the instructions of the food ministry, and there is, of course, the suggestion that if that condition continues until they get back to the natural system of marketing again there would be a preference shown probably for Danish bacon.
But the thing that is promoting Danish bacon to a much greater extent is what Canadians are doing themselves. If any member of this house were to go into Eaton's or Simpson's or any other of the larger stores tomorrow and order a parcel to be put up for delivery in Britain the parcel would in all probability be put up in Denmark and Danish bacon would be sent to Great Britain, paid for by a Canadian. That, of course, is one method of getting around the British regulation which says that you cannot advertise. We feel that the British are doing just what we ourselves would do under similar circumstances. The British have a situation where they are not able to feed their people as their people want to be fed and they must ration most of the food they are distributing. So the British authorities say: If we must distribute the food and tell our people this is what you have to take, we cannot at the same time permit others outside Great Britain to come in here and advertise urging our people to buy Canadian bacon instead of Danish or Danish bacon instead of Canadian; our people will have to take what we have to distribute to them. That is, I think, the only way in which the government can keep itself out of some difficulty, and this government or any other government would do the same thing under similar circumstances. That is what the British are doing. But we are helping the Danish to get around that when we walk into our stores and, instead of putting up a parcel ourselves and sending it to Britain, order and pay for a parcel to be made up in Denmark and sent to Britain from there. In almost any daily paper in Canada you will see advertisements of the products that can be sent to Britain from Denmark. I submit that if our Canadians assist in that advertising programme they are not helping Canada.
Was that practice not started because of the postal restrictions imposed by the government here?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; that movement started just as soon as the German troops were out of Denmark. We have had it stopped once or twice but it started up again. There is no way in which we can legally stop it.
There were restrictions all during the war and since on the kind of food we can send to Britain.
How do they get Canadian funds into Denmark to purchase this food?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am not going to
explain that. I had too much difficulty on the continent in getting money exchanged to try to explain how it is done. But they get paid for what they send.

Surely there is some way to stop it. We have a foreign exchange .control board with control over Canadian funds that are going abroad to be used abroad. Surely we are not going to lend the money to Denmark through some department of our government to enable them to carry on advertising against ourselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have tried to stop it and will continue to try, but we have not succeeded up to date.

I do not want to get into any argument about bacon. But I agree with the minister that this time he is right. I said once before in the house that I had been over there, and I am going to repeat what I said then, that the best bacon going to Britain today is Canadian. It is ahead of even the Danish product. I sympathize with my hon.

friend in our not being able to advertise over there. The only advertisement we have is when a British housewife gets good bacon and says, "That is the best we ever had," and I would1 always assure her that it was Canadian bacon she had that morning. Bacon that goes out in sliced form, no matter how you may advertise it, loses its identity when it gets there. I would be very sorry if this country, both east and west, fell down in bacon production, because we have a wonderful market in Britain. The people there want our bacon, and I hope we shall be able to maintain that market. ,
At page 102 of the estimates two bacon specialists are listed. What are their duties? Are they for the use of the meat board, or have they other functions?

speechtext: They are two inspectors, Doctor Miller and Major Leighton. I should like to ask a question as to the meat board protecting the farmer's produce. Some time ago the meat board announced that they would buy all the lambs at one-quarter of a cent less than the ceiling or the floor price, whichever you call it, and that was supposed to help the farmer. But it did not really help the farmer anyway, because the farmer sent his lambs to the stockyard or to the abattoir, and they paid just what they liked in a competitive market. It was only after the lambs were in the hands of the packing companies that that price came into operation. You have the same situation in regard to a carload of steers. I know what the minister's answer will be before he gives it, because he is going to say there are times when the farmer gets more than he is entitled to; but over a number of years I know that the

farmer is always on the wrong, side of the deal. If the packer pays more for something in one month or two months of the year, in the other ten months he pays less than he should. I wish to know if the minister has altered the policy of the meat board to give the farmer better protection than he has had in the past. I think the meat board is good, but it is only after the carcass is hung up by the heels that the price is considered. Something should be done on a hoof basis. They do it in other countries. I have seen it done in other countries. They bring the animal in and grade it, and when they hang it up by the heels there is not much difference in the grading. As it is today, the meat board is more help to the packing industry than to the farmer. Will the minister give me some information on it? The way it is done is not right.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think the hon. member knows as much about the transactions on the Winnipeg market as anyone; he has always been close to it and has had considerable to do with trading on it. He will agree that we have never had, up until the time we established the meat board, the same stability in prices over the years as we have had since the establishment of that board. Prior to the establishment of the meat board, our prices were quite high in July as a rule. It is true that they still go up to some extent in July, as do other markets, but only slightly when compared with what they did prior to the operations of the meat board. In the fall of the year when stock was coming off the pastures, and when farmers were getting a little anxious to get their hogs on. the market because the cold weather was coming, the market went down. In many years there was no limit to where it went. Then again we had difficulties when we started to put the finished cattle on the market in the spring of the year. For two or three years, and maybe three or four years after the bacon board, which eventually became the meat board, came into existence, there was a tendency on the part of everyone to say that we ought to provide a high price in July because it cost more, to feed hogs through the winter, to have them carried through the winter and delivered in June and July; and that we ought to provide for the price going down in the fall just as it did when the market was following the natural rules of supply and demand. We tried that for one year at the beginning of the war. We did not set seasonal prices, and we found out that on hogs it simply resulted in approaching what had always happened; when you had a volume your price went away down and when you did not have a volume your price went away up.

Supply-Agriculture
No one can gain by that method of marketing excepting the packer. He had the means of storing meat in cold storage from one period to another and he could benefit greatly by it. There was only one group of people in Canada who might have had any reason for saying that we should continue that, and they did. We did not continue it. We tried to establish a flat floor price at least for hogs and finally for cattle. It took us two years longer to persuade the cattle producers to agree that it ought to be done with cattle; but finally we were able to persuade them to agree to a fair price over the year, so that the farmer could get just about as high a return when he had a big volume to put on the market as he could get when he had a small volume to put on. We think it is beneficial to the farmer to stabilize the price over the whole year. We think, too, that it is a good thing for the farmer to extend that stabilization over two or three years. For that reason we have expanded these contracts from one year contracts into two and finally into three-year contracts in order to be sure that the price can be maintained above the floor over a longer period, or stabilized over a longer period. That is what the board is attempting to do and we think they have done it successfully. There have been very few times when the price has been below what would be the established floor. I think if you examine the records-I have them in front of me for anyone who shakes his head about it; I will read them if you wish-you will find that prices have remained almost at the same level for months back.
Has the minister any policy which will permit the meat board to buy these animals and kill them?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.
The minister has that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We bid on hogs, for example, and we have not had any serious difficulty about it. The hogs all go to some forty odd plants which are government inspected; that is, all the hogs on which we pay a premium, and these are the hogs that we desire to get 'for overseas shipment. Practically all of them go to some forty odd plants. It is a simple thing to go to forty odd plants, provided that you have authority behind' what you are doing, as we had under the War Measures Act and now have under the legislation which was passed this session. It is a simple thing to say to one of these plants, you must do what the others are doing, or to two or three plants, you must do what the others are doing. If we can say that, we
find we have no difficulty at all in getting the plants to cooperate in putting on to the domestic market what is required here, and putting on the British market the surplus. All of them are doing it in about the same proportion. Under that plan we have been able to get the hogs; but when it came to the cattle the situation was somewhat different. We had strong pressure, as I said, from producers, and more particularly from the larger producers, to set a price which was two cents lower in the fall than it was in the spring in order that cattle could be taken in and fed with the margin to begin with. We argued against that for about two years and finally got them, not exactly to agree, but to consent to trying out the other plan, which is working now. Here is how it operates, as the hon. member said a few moments ago. On the higher carcasses of beef we say we are prepared to buy every day at a certain price, which is only one-quarter of a cent below the ceiling. We are prepared to buy any time at a quarter of a cent below the ceiling all red and blue beef and send it to Britain. If the beef drops a quarter of a cent below the ceiling we get the beef that comes on the market during that period.
You buy only on a dead meat basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We are buying on a dead meat basis; that is the only place we can buy meat.
You could buy meat on the hoof if you wished to.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We could buy meat on the hoof, but I think it would be agreed that under the plan we are following beef is selling on the hoof at a higher level than it ever sold before.
It is never sold too high in the beef line.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is the argument, and I wish to correct what my hon. friend said a few moments ago. He said that the answer I was apt to give was that the farmer was getting all he was entitled to, anyway. I am a farmer. I never think that the farmer is getting all that he is entitled to. I think he ought to get more all the time.

I do not want to take up any more time. There is one thing the minister did not explain, namely, why we tried this two-eent scheme. I was one of the men on one of these boards when this two-cent system was tried out. We ran up against this. In a country so large as Canada there are many

types of farmers. There is the eastern farmer and the western farmer. You can feed steers in the west and sell them and find that the eastern farmer will buy them for as much as the packer will pay for them and then feed them on the grass farms in Ontario. The minister said that the westerner was offered the two eents more. You run up against a different type of farm in the east. They want to buy the steers cheap in the spring to put on these grass farms. There was a conflict of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The feeder who wanted to feed grain wanted to buy as cheap as he could in the fall so that he could sell at a profit in the spring. We have pretty well overcome both these things.

Has the minister taken into consideration the recommendations made by certain organizations in the west with regard to assisting in increasing hog production? There is no doubt that today the world needs hogs as badly perhaps as it did in 1944. If the farmer is to go through the work of growing barley and oats and raising hogs, staying with them day after day, particularly during the winter months so as to maintain production, and then finds at the end of that time that the amount of money he gets for his hogs as a result of doing all that laborious work in the winter is taken up in income tax, he will decide that it is not worth while. Has the minister taken into consideration the question of trying out for a period the granting of an immunity in respect of $400 or $500 of the farmer's first money received for hog production? It has been represented that if this were tried out the minister would find a great increase in hog production in the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In reply to that, I may say that the advertisement I am about to read gives what the farmer himself thinks about the matter. This is an advertisement put out by a cooperative in Alberta:
An appeal to the farmers of Canada and North America.

Supply-Agriculture
Grow another hog for Britain. Forward, Canadian farmers.
Join the live stock march to greater economic prosperity. Britain is hungry. Britain will pay. Britain can pay, Britain has paid. This is not another charity campaign. Today prosperity is a pig! That is one of the advertisements.
It is a Liberal ad.
We will all support that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
But that is not what my hon. friend was just saying. He is repeating the old story that if you gave somebody the right to produce without paying income -tax we would get more hogs. There are 138,000 farmers in Saskatchewan and only 7,958 of them paid income tax in the highest year of payment, which was last year, so that there are 130.000, or more than 130,000, who do not pay income tax. How will you get them to produce more hogs by deducting something from their income tax when they are not paying any? These farmers were not within $300 of the tax-free income that they will have this year, because the exemption was only $1,200 and now it is $1,500 for a married couple. Therefore they have to make another $300 in addition to what they made last year to get into the brackets at all.
The kind of campaign we want is the kind put on in Alberta with the support of the Alberta government and of the farmers and of this government. The thing for the farmers to do is to get into the income tax brackets instead of staying out of them. If every farmer were to produce what would enable him to get into the income tax brackets we would get our proportion of income in this country, and the sooner they get into those brackets the better for them. The government should not do anything to encourage them to stay out because they are not as well off when they are out. Let them get into the income brackets and it will be better for everyone, but particularly for the farmer.
They are not raising the hogs, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have brought them in from one per cent up to 3-7 per cent. We are getting along slowly, but we are getting along.
When will we be up to the 1944 production?

speechtext: Order.

I was going to say that the farmers in Prince Edward Island are taking a great interest in breeding a select class of hogs. For instance, only within the last two or three months they have shipped to Manitoba a carload or two of breeding stock. Buyers from Saskatchewan and Alberta are there now, but there is only one snag with reference to the selling of our breeding stock that is of a good quality. When those hogs are slaughtered, over sixty per cent of them are in the class A premium class. The demand for this stock is great. As I said, we have one snag, namely, the long freight haul from Prince Edward Island to Saskatchewan and Alberta. Will the minister take this as a suggestion, and consider giving an allowance on their freight rate to purchasers of this valuable stock which can be bought in Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
At present purebred
stock gets a freight rate of one-half. That is arranged for purebred stock all over the country. I want to agree with everything that has been said by the hon. member. Prince Edward Island stands right "at the top in the production of quality hogs. Their hogs are being utilized all across Canada to improve our hog population. I do not think anyone can say too much by way of eulogizing the effort which is being made there.

I realize, of course,
that there is a great variation in the number of days it takes a vessel to get across the
Supply-Agriculture

ocean. Can the minister give us, on the average, how many days it takes for the average cargo of bacon to go from Montreal to England? Can he also tell us how long it is held in storage in England before it goes out to the consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It takes about eight
days for the fastest boats that are carrying bacon across the ocean to make the trip. They are making it in about eight days. It is sometimes a little less than that and sometimes a little more, but it averages about that.
As to the matter of carrying the bacon in Britain, it is true that a few months ago- I would say a year ago-we had some difficulty in that there was a tendency to deliver in Britain freshly delivered bacon from Denmark. But there was an understanding entered into whereby the British bought only the heavy cured bacon from Denmark, the same as they were buying from Canada, in order that they could keep both Danish and Canadian bacon in storage for the same length of time. However, that difficulty is gradually disappearing; in fact, it has pretty much disappeared now. Britain is compelled at present to deliver to distributors over Britain practically all the bacon she gets as she gets it. That is partly because she is not getting as much from us as she got before and is not able to pile up storage that she utilizes in her rationing from time to time. I should also say that their transportation facilities have improved and their storage facilities are improving too.

Having regard to the
way in which Canadian bacon was marketed in Britain prior to the war and in view of the fact that in the near future we hope we can get back to the ordinary system of marketing our bacon in Britain, can the minister give us any idea as to this government's policy regarding the building of storages in England and the handling of Canadian bacon in the old country?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Both we and the British government would be tickled to death if we could get enough bacon to be able to store any. We cannot get it fast enough even to keep the rationing up to the level at which it ought to be kept. As a matter of fact, it has to be rationed very low by Britain. There is not any possibility of building up any storage at the present time, either on this side or on the other side.
Is the government going to wait until the last minute to think about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We have been thinking about it during the twelve years I have been

here, and we did a considerable amount about it before the war. We did a good deal about it in the first year of the war when Britain did not really want our bacon at all. We stirred them up to the extent of being able to sell them some fifty million pounds more than they wanted to take, in the second year of the war. But since that time they have been wanting far more than we can give them.

Was it rented storage
that was used or were there Canadian facilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The storage we used
in the early part of the war was blown all to pieces in 1940. It was not there at all, and it has to be reestablished.

Was that storage
Canadian owned?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

Smithfield market was
bombed. The storages along the Thame* were completely destroyed during the first big raid that was made by the German air force. Those facilities have not yet all been put back, but they will be in due course.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. Canadians did not own any storage. But it does not make much difference who owns it, as long as it can be utilized to full capacity. I did not know that my hon. friend was a socialist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When these estimates were before the committee previously I wished to make a few remarks but was unable to do so. Some of what I have to say will be of a critical nature, but before going on with that I should like to thank the minister for the announcement he made in the house on May 19 in connection with federal assistance to the Montreal neurological institute. I happened to be in Montreal in January visiting one of my
Supply-Health and Welfare

constituents who was a patient there. While I was in the city, I happened to see a copy of the Montreal Standard containing a feature story outlining the critical financial position of this internationally known institute. Perhaps I might read a portion of it:
Staff members at the neurological institute are mixing their neurology these days with discussions of the financial difficulties which have put the institute close to bankruptcy. The MNI faces a bleak future unless more money is forthcoming, and soon. Otherwise, the institute will be forced to close the hospital unit by April of this year. The MNI is owned by McGill university and, in certain aspects of its clinical activity, the Royal Victoria hospital acts as its agent.
My friend, who had been to Rochester previously, was extravagant in his praise of the neurological institute in Montreal; and I am very happy to learn that the minister and other members of the cabinet have regarded this as a national institute and that an adequate financial grant is to be made. I am sure that when the supplementary estimates come before the house hon. members in all sections will unanimously support the government in this wise decision.
Having said that, I consider that the minister is open to criticism because of his failure to place the problem of health in its proper perspective. The other evening the hon. member for Lanark gave an interesting address, outlining some of the major problems. Most of his material was not new; it was brought to the attention of the country in 1943, prior to the last election. I looked up some of the evidence given before the social security committee, and I find that on Friday, March 19, 1943, the late Doctor Heagerty gave evidence before that committee outlining the position in Canada. He said:
We have been losing an average of a thousand mothers each year. It is down a little during the last two or three years, due to the concentrated efforts of the provincial departments of health. When a mother dies, the child usually dies. The child dies because there is no one to take care of the child. We would like to have incubators-to take the newborn child to the hospital we haven't got them and we cannot et them, we have no money for them. Why ave we this condition? We have been losing over the past ten years on an average of 15,000 children under one year of age each year.
Then he referred to the situation in regard to tuberculosis:
And now, _what is the situation in regard to tuberculosis in the various provinces of Canada? Can you do anything about tuberculosis? Well, you take Quebec and Ontario. They are very very close together. They have the same air, very much the same living conditions* and you find that the death rate in Ontario'is 25, as compared with 80 in Quebec. Why is that? Ontario has provided practically free treatment, 
it is now X-raying all the people of the province at a cost of 30 cents per X-ray. In Saskatchewan the death rate is twenty-nine. Free treatment is provided in Saskatchewan.
There are three provinces which have adequate facilities for the prevention and treatment of tuberculosis; they are Saskatchewan, Ontario and Alberta.
I might mention that this interesting information was compiled prior to the last election. The present administration created the impression that they really planned on doing something about the health problem in Canada. I find that on April 29, 1946, in outlining the government's proposals before the dominion-provincial conference the Prime Minister made this suggestion in the field of health regarding planning grants. He said:
The dominion will pay to any provincial government which so desires immediately upon completion of the agreement, $5,000 plus five cents per capita of its 1941 population (but not less than $15,000) to be spent within two years on studies of the requirements of the province in the field of essential medical, hospital and related services. Quarterly reports would be submitted by the provincial governments.
Then there is a paragraph on health insurance, another on health grants and another on hospital construction.
I find that the present Minister of National Defence, who was then the Minister of National Health and Welfare, outlined in greater detail the government's proposals in the field of national health. He recognized definitely that there are great inequalities in the quantity and quality of. health care available in different parts of Canada, and in the* cost* of such public and private health services and medical and hospital facilities as were then available. He continued:
These inequalities in part reflect differences-in personal incomes, and in part are due to differences between rural and urban areas. Great differences between provinces arise from these same factors.
Then, to give an indication of what the government planned to do, he said:
To remove the disparities in standards of health services in different parts of Canada, to avoid the risks of sudden heavy expenditures, and distribute health costs more widely and equitably, and above all, to obtain the benefits of better health for the great majority of our people-these are the objects of the proposals which the federal government is now making with respect to health insurance for all, and increased public health services assisted by federal grants.
The minister went on to outline the grant for planning and organization, health insurance proposals, and different benefits to be made available for fighting tuberculosis,.

Supply-Health and Welfare
mental disease, venereal disease, aids for crippled children, and moneys for professional training.
It is not good enough for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to come before the committee and make the sort of speech he made the other night when discussing the problem of cancer. What the minister said was of general interest; but when he had finished he had not told us how much the federal government is planning on spending to fight this dread disease. The hon. member for Lanark drew attention to the fact that we have had about half a million dollars tied up in a fund for about twelve years, and that that is a fund which does not belong to the federal government.
The major part of the minister's speech was devoted to the setting up of a national cancer institute for Canada. He mentioned that this institute is not responsible to this or any other government. If the minister is so concerned about cancer he should be prepared to make an adequate grant to see that the necessary scientific personnel will be trained and will be made available in different parts of Canada to fight the disease. The amount of 8150,000 a year for the next few years is just a drop in the bucket when one considers the cost measured in lives caused by this disease in Canada.
I suggest that the minister, in introducing the item, should have made a statement indicating that he is now calling the ministers of public health from the provinces, and that he is prepared to recommend to the cabinet that the federal government now enter into an agreement with those provincial governments which have been able to reach agreement with the federal government in the matter of dominion-provincial relations.
I need not remind the committee that when the matter of old age pensions was introduced we did not wait until all the provinces were agreed at one time to introduce legislation for old age pensioners. We had old age pensions in some of the provinces for almost ten years before the benefits were claimed by other provinces.
I suggest that if the minister wishes to bring the premiers of Ontario and Quebec to reason, all he has to do is to announce that, if they want to, the other seven provinces will be able to go along with the federal government in carrying out the objectives which were outlined at the dominion-provincial conference, and that grants will be made for those services which were discussed at the conference.
May I mention that in my own province of Saskatchewan we have taken the federal proposals seriously, and we are proceeding to extend public services in many different directions. Hospital services legislation, the first of its kind on this continent, has been introduced in Saskatchewan. The experience we are having will be useful to other provinces in Canada, and it is hardly fair that, with our limited resources, Saskatchewan should be asked to bear all the expense in connection with this essential educational work which must be undertaken before any part of Canada can proceed with an over-all hospital or health services programme.
Then there is the matter of providing an adequate number of doctors, dentists and nurses. The hon. member for Lanark referred to the shortage of nurses. In some of the evidence presented by the federal government during the war, it was recognized that there are places in Canada where lack of medical services has placed the people living in those communities in an unfair position. When war breaks out, people in all the provinces are expected to offer their lives in the service of their country. If in some parts of the dominion there are young people who are rejected on physical grounds, that is a national misfortune. So in peace time I believe it should be our objective and goal to see that in all parts of Canada we should have a sufficient number of doctors, dentists andi nurses adequately to care for the people.
In the national health survey conducted by the Canadian medical procurement and assignment board during the war, we found that provinces with the lowest average incomes had the lowest number of doctors, and that in those provinces doctors had to travel greater distances over worse roads. In Ontario where the average income is highest there was one doctor for every 872 persons. In Saskatchewan where, in 1931, the income was down to $285 per capita there was one doctor for every 1,578 persons. The experience in my constituency has been that when the young people from there have attended medical colleges in Montreal, Toronto or Winnipeg they have established contacts while in college and have found it easier to practise medicine away from the communities in which they lived. The result has been that we have never been able to attract a sufficient number of professional people to that area to serve the population. At the present time our ratio is one doctor for 3,300 persons. In the Canadian army the ratio was something more than four doctors per 1,000, while in the United States it was even higher.
In most civilized countries it is considered that there should be at least one doctor for every 1,000 or 1,500 of population. While we are making some progress in Saskatchewan in attracting doctors to practise in that province,
Supply-Health and Welfare

we shall not be able with our own resources to train a sufficient number, nor shall we be able to provide the type of medical and hospital services that a country with the great resources possessed by Canada, should offer.
The same is true with regard to dental services. The boundaries of the constituency I represent will be defined in the redistribution measure, and we shall then have only one dentist for some 48,000 persons. At present we have three dentists in the area, in the ratio of one dentist to 19,000 people. The redistribution will take two of those dentists out of the area, and one of them is about to retire. While Saskatchewan is offering inducements to dentists to come to our province, we have not a dental college and hospital, and our young people have to go east or west to get their dental education and too many of them do mot return to the province.
I was interested in a study made by Doctor Clare Robinson in the field of providing medical education. Doctor Robinson is from Queen's university. He points out what is generally known, but I think the statistics will come as a surprise to a great many. He tells us, for example, that although thirty-six per cent of our people in Canada give agriculture as their occupation, only 12-2 per cent of our doctors come from this group. From finance we get over five per cent of our doctors. We have four per cent of our population in the professional groups and they supply twenty-eight per cent of our doctors. Doctor Robinson goes on to explain that a great many of our children have not much chance of ever becoming medical doctors under the present set-up. He mentions that earlier in the century it was possible for people to work their way through university, but that nowadays, with the cost of university education rising every year, it is next to impossible for young people, regardless of their mental qualifications, to find the wherewithal to get through university. A chart shows the cost of medical education. He says that if you want an expensive medical education choose McGill, and the next most expensive universities are Toronto and Dalhousie, where averages of $975 and $974 were reported. Next comes Montreal. The universities where you can start taking your university course at the lowest cost are the western universities, the university of Saskatchewan with an annual cost of $628, and the university of Alberta with $698, as compared with $1,206 at McGill university.

speechtext:
It was $698 as compared with $1,206 for McGill and $975 for Toronto. In war time it was considered a national responsibility to train personnel for the air force, army and navy. I recall that the Minister of National Defence for Air told the house that it cost $25,000 to train a pilot for the air force, $27,000 for an observer and $28,000 for a navigator. It costs $5,000 to train a medical doctor, Doctor Robinson says. If we could spend $25,000 to train young Canadians by the thousands in the art of war it should not be a problem to find $5,000 to train an adequate number of people as doctors and dentists. It is very difficult for me to explain to the veterans in my constituency that Canada was able to supply one dentist for every 500 soldiers in war time and that now we have only one dentist for 44,000 or 45,000 people in peace time. It is not fair to say that this is a provincial responsibility, that the province should bear the cost. The students who graduate from these colleges are free to practise in any part of the dominion if they pass the dominion examinations. In war time the problem of financing the war was a national responsibility. In peace time the fighting of disease should claim a larger percentage of our total national income than has been the case. So I suggest that the minister should, without further delay, convene a conference of dominion and provincial health authorities and reach an agreement with those provinces which are prepared to go along and carry out the spirit of the decisons reached by the previous Minister of National Health and Welfare, so that a programme can be carried out that would be satisfactory to the dominion and provinces concerned. I am sure that the great volume of evidence placed before the social security committee before the last election demonstrates that health is a national concern.
I was particularly interested in the brief "Health on the March" presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. There are some striking paragraphs in the proposals submitted by the federation. For example:
(a)	The large majority of the people are unable to pay for adequate medical care with its rapidly increasing scope and costs; while at the same time, those who give the services are not receiving a just remuneration. This state of affairs is having a serious effect on the welfare of our dominion.
(b)	Health is a national problem which is becoming more and more evident under the stress of war conditions. The responsibility of

Supply-Health and Welfare
the federal government in calling on man and woman power from all classes entails federal responsibility for the people's health.
(c) A national health plan would encourage a strong national sentiment. Confederation was intended to foster a national economy. There is now urgent need to revive this interest.
They make recommendations how they would organize and find the wherewithal, a system of financing that would be equitable so far as the individuals are concerned, and they propose nine different methods of raising funds. They suggest that a fund should be raised by the federal authorities, that the plan should include all citizens, not merely those who can afford the luxury of good health, and they say:
Complete coverage is necessary to achieve financial soundness and to spread the cost equitably.
They go on to say that the promotion of positive health and the prevention of disease should be the primary purpose of the plan. I am not insisting that the minister should accept the plans which the members of this group have emphasized or the plan of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, but I submit it is imperative that the government's own proposals made to the provinces should now be presented again to the seven provinces which have made financial agreements with the government; the minister should be able to persuade members of the cabinet that an adequate budget for health should be provided, and his officers and his department should fight disease in peace time with the same imagination and the same determination as we fought it in war time.

A start has already been made on certain films previously recommended by the dominion council of health, a body which meets twice a year at the instance of the Department of National Health and Welfare to discuss matters of mutual and national interest.
