Certain films were suggested as a result of the health education conference last fall and are now under active consideration. This= will include such subjects as the common cold, immunization and tuberculosis. It w hoped that we shall be able to get on as quickly as possible with the scripting and shooting of a number of these films under this year's budget, but it will be necessary to' provide for a carryover of a considerable-quantity of work next year. This we feel will be adequately covered for the time by $32,000 requested, which it is thought is sufficient to produce two such films.
On the general item of public information, I did feel at the outset that there were some items which could be eliminated; for instance, one telling people how to ski. One of the first instructions I gave was that there be no further moneys expended on that publication. I must say at this stage, however, that my review of the educational work of the department convinces me that if we are to do the job which hon. gentlemen generally believe we should pursue, an assignment with which I am in full accord, we must take the suggestion of the hon. member for Lanark, who last year took issue with some of his own colleagues in saying that rather than curtail information we ought to extend it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I believe that is a sound view to take. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to criticize this item, which has been reduced considerably from the sum of over $590,000 to $390,000. I am bound to say that at -the moment my view is that that is a curtailment, to which perhaps I would not have consented earlier in the year had I
Supply-Health and Welfare

known as much about my work as I do now. I say that quite honestly and frankly. If we are to bring home the facts to the people of this country, in pursuance of the constitutional responsibilities of this government in the matter of health, we should not hesitate wisely to bring home, in as graphic a manner as we can to all groups of the population, rural and urban, the steps which it is thought by our technical staff should be taken to improve the standards of health of the Canadian people.
We have heard a discussion tonight, an admirable discussion thus far, though not too complimentary to a minister who is doing his best within a short time to tackle the great responsibility that devolves upon him. We have heard suggestions tonight about a cutting down in maternity mortality rates, infant mortality rates, deaths resulting from tuberculosis, cancer and the like-all of them projects that cannot help but capture the imagination and the interest of any responsible minister-and I think I can say this to the membership of a house that knows my interest in these things. I feel keenly that we should do some of the things about which mention has been made tonight, and one of the ways of doing this is to bring the matter home to the people of the country.
Take the work of industrial health. We can bring home the importance of this to the men who work in our factories, pointing out ways and means of improving health standards. Take the work of Doctor E. Couture, whose book, "The Canadian Mother and Child" has now reached a total circulation of over 750000 copies. That kind of work is having an incalculable benefit. I have looked through carefully the criticisms which were leveled last year, responsibly directed criticisms I know, but which perhaps were made without a full knowledge of the facts. I must say that, having gone into the items carefully, I can find only a genuine demand throughout the country, from all kinds of groups, for the kind of publication we are putting out.
No two people will agree on what is the wise way of bringing home to the public information in regard to problems of health and the ways and means of meeting health deficiency. We must put ourselves at the disposal of those who, through radio or films or by writing, or through other methods of graphic portrayal, feel that these are the most effective ways of dealing with the matter. Take the question of press fillers. I am not convinced by the argument of the hon. member for Eglinton. I have been trying to find some way of agreeing with him, but I regret

to say that I have not found one item on which I am fully in accord with him.
These press fillers go, not only to the daily press, but to the weekly press as well, and I find that there are literally thousands of letters coming to the department from men and women on our farms and in our factories, workers and others, asking for further information of the kind disseminated by some of these films and fillers. I can only say that in my judgment they serve a useful purpose, and rather than complain about the quantity, perhaps we should be open to some suggestion with regard to increasing them.
A trial survey of the press some months ago convinced me that a widespread use of these educational fillers is a wise assignment. Newspapers large and small are slipping them in where they have space. Some of the most influential newspapers in Canada, such as the Toronto Globe and Mail, a well known Canadian paper, the Ottawa Journal, the Montreal Gazette, use them frequently.

Do not forget the
Windsor Star.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
And the Windsor Star, Canada's first newspaper. In fact some of the larger newspapers have asked for more copy along the same line. The Montreal Star arranged for us to provide a continuous service on health hints to be used in connection with one of its special feature pages. The Northern Ontario called for additional material to feature on its woman's page. Editors of house organs and trade journals have asked to be included in the service.
I had a case brought to my attention only yesterday. The bulletin of the department had an issue on cancer about two or three weeks ago. From a nearby community not many miles from this city, a doctor wrote in telling us that he had left that at the home of a woman whom he was attending in connection with another malady. The pamphlet was lying in the home. The husband read it. As hon. gentlemen may recall, in that pamphlet there was a suggestion that an examination for cancer should be undertaken whenever any apparent symptom appeared or there was any thought of it on the part of the potential victim. This person read that health bulletin and went to a doctor, who is a member of this house. As a result of his diagnosis, this doctor found that the person had cancer in an early stage. I sincerely hope that as a result of that doctor's care, and the diagnosis which was immediately made, that particular individual may be relieved of the dreadful malady. That is one example. One could go on.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I can only say that I am convinced beyond peradventure of the wisdom of the department's programme. At the request of hon. gentlemen earlier in the session I tabled a list of the publications of this particular division. If there is any item to which any hon. gentleman takes exception, I shall be prepared to discuss it, argue as to its merits and deal with it right on the floor of this house.

I wish to say something in connection with this general administration. I want to congratulate the minister on the degree he got at Michigan university. He appears to be getting extremely popular by degrees. I visited Detroit a few years ago when Mayor Cousens was mayor of that city, just about the time of the discovery by Doctor Banting, who hung out his shingle in Toronto after his graduation from Varsity, and another medical student called Mr. Charlie Best, who was a joint discoverer of this great boon to humanity. At that time I was in Detroit city addressing the Canadian club in 1923 and I found fifty doctors there from the universities of this country, McGill, Queen's, Toronto and other universities. When I came back as a young member of the House of Commons, I had a long connection with public health, with the hospital system and the development of the hospital system in our city. We brought Doctor Hastings, a great health officer, into the Department of Public Health. At that time there were so many cases of typhoid and diphtheria that we had to get a new sewage system, a new water supply system, chlorination and filtration of water, inspection of milk and all that kind of thing. An ounce of prevention was found to be worth a pound of cure. I do not wish to interfere with other hon. gentlemen who desire to speak in this debate, but I just wish to bring two or three matters to the attention of the government.
The young minister has shown a great deal of activity since he joined this department. I do not altogether like a lawyer in his position. He is good at the law business, but a lawyer at the head of the health department is another matter. Once in a while I become ill and send for the best doctor I can get. I wish to point out to the government that we are losing a great many of the graduates in medicine from our universities. They are not staying here but are going to the United States. I found this to be true of the great Johns Hopkins medical school at Baltimore, before I came into this parliament; the head chairs were occupied by Canadians. There were Doctor Howard Kelly, Doctor Thomas Cullen, Doctor Llewellyn Barker, Doctor
Sweetman and those great men who brought medicine to the distinguished position it had in that university succeeding the greater Doctor Osier who went to Oxford. I brought before the house on February 27, 1923, this question of a large annuity to our scientists because I saw this general exodus. Doctor Banting was going to go to the states. Mr. Best was then a medical student. A great many of the medical students of our country are poor people, and have had to struggle to get a degree. I venture to say ninety per cent of them are poor people. I know that one of the doctors-I do not want to give his name- took menial positions on boats in the summer, sold papers and did all kinds of things in the summer months in order to earn money for the fees. In the faculty of medicine the fees have been going up in geometrical progression, two, four, six, eight. You need to be a rich man to be a doctor.
I wish to point out one or two things. On February 27, 1923. I spoke on this matter. I have the Hansard debates here but I will not read it all. I referred to the history of medicine, where all these discoveries which have been made in medicine down through the ages were made by people who never made a nickel out of them but gave their lives to science in the way that Doctor Banting and Mr. Best gave theirs. They got only a small amount of money from the government. If we want to do something, the Canadian government has got to be up and doing. There is no use in our having a skeleton department and turning the matter over to the municipalities and the provinces. It should be made a federal matter entirely. They have that in England, Germany, and France; they have a national system of health. It is the duty of the government to look after the health, wealth and happiness and prosperity of its people. Life has no object at all unless a person has good health.
Look at the poor Indians in this country, people who are not even citizens. We have spent two sessions trying to find out if they are citizens. If they are citizens, and they should have been fifty years ago, they are entitled to health laws. We have taken two sessions to find anything out about it. If you look down the history of medicine you will find that the discoveries of medical men to cure disease have been given to the world freely, without fee or reward, such as antiseptics which were given freely to the world by Lord Lister, anaesthesia bj' Simpson and Morton, vaccination by Jenner, and many others. For the most part, they never made anything out of them at all. There was only one case I think, where it was capitalized in
Supply-Health and Welfare

Germany, the discovery of what was called 606 by Erlich. Burdock's blood bitters and all those quack medicines which people buy unnecessarily in many cases are a commercial matter. There is one country which has done something, and that is France, where they honour men of science. If you go to Paris you will see monuments and parks called after Pasteur. Here in this country we have forgotten about these men. The other day I saw the grave of Doctor Banting in Mount Pleasant cemetery. There was a small monument on it about the size of this desk, made of concrete, with the word "Banting" on it. We do not want all our bright scholars to go to the United States. I call attention to the debate away back on February 27, 1923, where I introduced a resolution asking a grant of $7,500 for Doctor Banting and one for Doctor Best. The government of the day said they could not do anything then. I like to give credit where credit is due. Away back in June, 1923, I called attention to the fact that in the supplementary estimates Doctor Banting was given an annual grant of $7,500, and I said Doctor Best should be given an equal grant. That discussion will be found in the debates of this house at page 4439 of Hansard for June 27, 1923; and I also discussed the matter on February 27 of the same year. That was a creditable action on the part of the government. It led to the establishment of the Banting institute. At that time I was at the Johns Hopkins hospital, and I was informed by one of the leading doctors there that at that time they had nearly nine hundred thousand cases of diabetes in the United States. I do not know where we would have been in the second war had it not been for that great discovery.
I hope we may have a national policy in regard to medicine. I do not mean state medicine; I am not referring to that. For one thing I believe internes in our hospitals should be given $600 a year as well as living expenses. That would not be very much. Then there is the question of nurses. Four sessions ago, when you could not get a nurse, when they were not available, I asked what the government was going to do about it. They have not done very much, and the same difficulty still exists.
I might mention many other matters tonight, but I urge upon the government that these men of science should be kept in Canada, and that our universities should be given large grants of money. Instead of building up a great central health department here, I believe certain universities could take up different branches of this work, including the work on cancer; and they should have federal assistance

by large capital grants all along the line. The King George V cancer fund is now pretty well gone; by the end of this year there will be very little money left in the treasury, and I think the government should give a very large grant for that purpose. I believe the day is not far distant when we shall need a national health policy for this country. The housing situation is simply ridiculous, and it leads to a great deal of poor health in regard! to water supply and sewage disposal. I remember back in 1914 and 1915, when the late John Ross Robertson did such magnificent work in Toronto in connection with the sick children's hospital, Which has been a blessing to the children of our city and province ever since. At that time the question of medical and dental inspection in the schools came up, and we were the first city to have that service, which has since been extended to the secondary schools. So I hope the government will come to the assistance of the municipalities by means of substantial grants. Perhaps this should be done through the provinces, but the provinces seem to like to hang on to the money. I believe the government should do something for the hospital system of the whole country in order to help out the municipalities, because this represents a serious drain on real estate and the cost is going up by leaps and bounds.
I know other hon. gentlemen wish to take part in this debate, but I want to impress upon the government that something must be done to keep our young scientists at home, the way France and the United States and Germany have done for many years past. After all is said and done, we can take a lesson from what was done by the German people before the war in regard to medicine and many other branches of science, though no doubt some of them went too far. Instead of marking time, I believe we should have a large fund, perhaps $25,000,000 to start with, among other things for research into medical matters by Canadian students in our own universities; and we should also see to it that our university graduates in medicine are not exported to the United States.

To go back to the question of education, I agree that education, or propaganda put out fo the people, is one of the most effective weapons we have. I think that piece of literature on the cancer programme was one of the finest things I have ever seen. It is unfortunate that in an item which appears further down in the list the minister has had to cut expenditures on child and maternal health from $80,000 to approximately $46,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It is not as bad as it seems. That was as the result of not providing for a

Supply-Health and Welfare
film such as that which was completed last year. When we come to that item we can deal with it.

Excellent work has been done under this item. I do not think a finer piece of work than Doctor Couture's book "Mother and Child" has ever been put out by any department of health. Some of the things put out under this educational policy are the very best, but some things still creep in that are very foolish. I have mentioned Doctor Couture's book, and now I will go from the sublime to the ridiculous. Here is a filler which I think must have been written by a sailor. He has it headed, "Woolies Away", he must have been thinking of "Anchors Aweigh." In it he warns the people of the country to have their woolies cleaned, because if they do not they are liable to get vermin. This may contain scientific facts, but I do not think it is any great contribution to Canadian literature. I want to point out that some of this ridiculous propaganda is still included in the fillers sent out to the newspapers. I criticized this practice last year. There has been a great improvement since then, but I think there is room for still further improvement.
When the minister was speaking he mentioned industrial hygiene.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I will give them now. With respect to item 201, the estimate for 1947-48 is $143,727, whereas in 1946-47 it was $226,537. The expenditures for 1946-47 amounted to $89,421.74. The unliquidated commitments for 1946-47 are $13,437.11. The total commitments for 1946-47 are $102,858.85.

That is just the reason why I think it is so important that we have the actual expenditures. Last year the minister asked for an appropriation of more than $226,000. He has actually spent or contracted
Supply-Health and Welfare

to spend $102,000. That indicates how different the estimates and the expenditures can be. I am sure the minister spent everything he felt it necessary to spend under the item. And yet we find that only about forty per cent of the amount of money he persuaded parliament last year to put at his disposal in respect of this item has been spent.
Surely we do not need any better example of the need for some better method of checking the estimates of these departments. This is the first example we have reached tonight. I have not the slightest doubt that the ministers-and when I say "the ministers" I mean ministers who have been in office from time to time; there have been two of them in the last year-* expended everything on that item they considered should be spent. It shows that last year parliament was imposed upon when it was asked to put $226,000 at the disposal of the department in respect of this item. We need no better proof of the fact that we ought to have, in respect of every item coming before the committee of supply, the actual expenditures in the preceding fiscal year on the item. The estimate of the previous year is no guide. Anyone running a business would insist upon the actual expenditures. Will the minister be good enough to furnish similar information on the other items?
Let me point out that, whereas hon. members talk about reductions in expenditures, what the committee is faced with in respect of this item is an increase in expenditures. It is all very well to bring before us in print these estimates which show reductions in estimated expenditures. Looking at this item, one sees what appears to be a handsome reduction of $82,810 from the appropriated amount for last year. But when one looks into it and finds what was actually spent, he finds that the department is asking the committee this year to provide $41,000 more than was actually spent last year.
Let us not be misled by what appear to be reductions in the estimates. Let us remember that when reductions appear they are only reductions as compared with the estimated expenditures of the preceding year, and have nothing to do with actual expenditure. We do not need any further proof of the fact that the way in which parliament is going about the task of checking expenditures is little better than a farce.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to what the hon. member has said. He has told me privately and in a kindly fashion his views on the subject. He will appreciate the task any government or business has to esti-

A few days ago a return was tabled showing that there were two stations in Canada where lepers are taken care of, one at Tracadie in New Brunswick, and one at Bentinck island in British Columbia. In the former station there are some seven patients kept in a special ward of a hospital at a cost of something over $8,000 for the year. At Bentinck island there are three who have been maintained for an expenditure of roughly $5,000 for the year. Those two figures have' been constant over the past ten years.
I should like to offer the suggestion that it is an unnecessary expenditure to maintain these two stations, and that a saving could be made by their amalgamation. I know something about the situation in British Columbia because the station there is in my constituency. It is located on an island where the unfortunate patients live. For a number of years there have been only two. I believe one was a Chinaman and one was a Jap. The great unhappiness that these individuals experience is the loneliness of that station. If, for instance, the seven were moved from New Brunswick to that island I do not think the cost would go up very much, because there is ample accommodation for them on that island and they are cared for from the quar-

With regard to penicillin and our own laboratories, the methods of assaying penicillin have been studied carefully. There are now known to be at least four types or fractions of penicillin with varying therapeutic efficiency. I am able to say-and this is by way of tribute to our own laboratory-that a Canadian standard penicillin has been prepared and is distributed to manufacturers for control of their production. This service administers part V of the Canada Shipping Act, sick mariners and marine hospitals, to provide such medical, surgical and other treatment as the case requires to any sick mariner employed on board and belonging to a ship which has paid sick mariners dues during the current calendar year.
Revenue is obtained by a compulsory levy on the registered tonnage of a ship arriving in any port in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Ediward Island, British Columbia and Manitoba and Ontario on Hudson bay or James bay.
Applications for treatment are approved by the local collector of customs, who is also responsible for the collection of dues. Payment is made prior to the first fishing voyage of each season.
Vessels engaged in the coasting trade within the limits of one province are exempt from the payment of dues; also vessels arriving at any port in the province of Quebec from any port in the province of Ontario.

Clinics, under full time medical officers of the division are maintained at Vancouver, B.C., Quebec, P.Q., Sydney, N.S., Halifax, N.S., and Saint John, N.B. speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me I might try to save time by saying that this is a new effort, and when that estimate was conceived the staff had not even, been selected. That is the main reason for the lower expenditure. I only say this because I think I anticipate the tenor of his argument and am trying to economize on time.
I still would like to offer this brief comment. The answer given by the minister is substantially the same as that given by his predecessor in 1946 and 1945. In each case it was a new branch.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It could not have been in 1945, because the branch was only authorized in September of that year. No, pardon me, I am in error.

We had it before us in the session of 1945, and wei made provision for it. The programme outlined then was the same as the programme outlined now; and we were told the same thing, in 1946. If the minister seriously expects that he will have occasion to spend $211,000 wisely on this work, then I think this committee is prepared to hear his case and make the money available if he proves his case. But a great deal more will have to be usefully done than was done last year with an expenditure of $63,000. What is being asked this year is three and a half times what was actually spent last year. Is this programme developing now to the point where an expenditure three and a half times greater than that of the fiscal year recently ended is to be required?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Every endeavour will be made to spend it properly, to realize the objectives and carry out the functions of the division.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.

What was the expenditure under this item, please?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The estimate for 1946-47 was $162,992. The expenditure for 1946-47 was $132,343, with unliquidated commitments for the same period of $6,087.07.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I just want to make the comment again that it seems to me there are too many reductions of too large an amount in the estimates for educational and informational publicity. I fear there is false economy, and I hope the minister will make sure that we are not losing something, in connection with a matter like nutrition, by cutting down on these expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I give my full assurance that the reduction does not in any way affect the purposes the hon. member and I have in mind.

Just on that point, I think it would be of interest to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if at some appropriate time the minister would give us the actual expenditure, during the fiscal year just closed, on educational and informational publicity, as it is now called, or publicity and information as it was called last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I will do that.
The figures I gave earlier this evening were the estimated expenditures, not the actual amount spent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I said I would do that.
Just a moment. I think it may be interesting to see whether the minister is really budgeting for a reduction in expenditure, as compared with the actual expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The minister is definitely budgeting for wise expenditure-
I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: -or for a reduction, whatever you wish me to say.
I think there must have been something wrong with the budgeting last year, if I may say a word in support of what my deskmate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, has said1.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have just explained that it does not represent any reduction in functions. Eleven thousand dollars of the amount asked for last year was to meet a commitment carried over from the previous year. My hon. friend may be sure I am not going to reduce this division if I can possibly avoid doing so.
Would the minister tell us the actual expenditures on edhcational and informational publicity last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes; $278,326.84.

That cannot be right, for there is an amount of only $61,627 shown in the estimates.

speechtext: You want the break-down?
No. How much of the $61,000 allocated last year was spent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Would you just let that stand so that we can pass on? I will give the information before the estimates are through.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National health branch-
Combating venereal diseases-
21-i. Administration, $37,875.

I note that the estimate for administration has been reduced by nearly $9,000, and it was not very large in the first place. Is the venereal disease situation so well under control that any lessening of the activity of the department is justified?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: As my hon. friend will know, this matter is primarily one which comes under the provincial authorities. Our interest in the matter is under section 5 of the National Health and Welfare Act, referring to supplementary assistance and coordination. The decreases do not represent anything in the way of fundamental functions, but are rather represented by transfer of personnel. For instance, in respect of one position for a medical specialist, advertised during October, 1946, it was found that of many applicants no one was judged to have the required qualifications. The position will be re-advertised with some revision of qualifications in the hope that it may be filled in the forthcoming fiscal year. That accounts, in part, for the item of $8,400.

That means you will not have that specialist this year. I note that the bureau of statistics now reports in respect of these diseases, and I also note in the annual report for the year ended March 31, 1946- and I believe that is the last available-that the figures for 1945 are higher than those for 1944. Has the minister the figures for 1946?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
There is some difficulty in giving those figures. My hon. friend is quite right when he refers to the bureau of statistics. But this is the Department of National Health and Welfare, and my officers take the position-and I must say I believe they are correct-that because these reports are not complete it would be giving an erroneous picture for the Department of National Health and Welfare, on what is not a complete report to give figures which might be misleading. That is the position my officials
think w;e should take, and I think perhaps it is the proper one.

The department has at
least gone so far as to give figures. I do not say they are considered as being absolutely accurate. They realize that all these cases are not reported. But how are people to have a knowledge and understanding of the danger of these diseases unless they have statistics which will give them that information? If it is proper to give a figure for 1944-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That is a figure from the
dominion bureau of statistics. To the extent they are helpful, our department uses those figures. However I have indicated that it is a matter of incomplete reporting. That is not the fault of the bureau of statistics; rather, it is the fault of reporting agencies throughout the country. An attempt is being made to try to perfect the system of reporting to a central office, so that we can be in a position to give a much more accurate set of figures.

I did not ask the minister if the figures were those from his own department. I asked if he had similar figures. Has he figures for the year 1946 which will compare with these for 1944 and 1945? The question is a simple one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
want the figures from the bureau of statistics?

Yes, if you have them,
for 1946. The bureau of statistics figures are the ones I have before me.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I will give them for 1946,
as they are given by the dominion bureau of statistics; but I want to emphasize clearly that that is the source from which these figures come. The total venereal disease cases in 1946 is placed at 41,556. The reason I hesitate, as my hon. friend will understand, is that I cannot say too strongly that these are not based on a complete report.

But there is no note to
that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
But that is the figure by
the bureau of statistics, not of this department.

But I have before me
the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946. It begins with a letter addressed to His Excellency the Governor General, and states:
May it please Your Excellency:

Brooke Claxton,
Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Supply-Health and Welfare

I wonder what the minister has in mind. Has he no confidence in the report of his department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I have. My hon. friend
knows me better than that.
I am afraid I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Well, this particular
minister has taken the position I have stated tonight on the advice of those in the department who, I think, are in a position to advise. And in taking that position, I take it in the belief that it is the proper thing to do. I cannot say more than that. Should I give a report next year, my hon. friend will have to compare it in the light of what he has just read.

Let us go into this
farther. I understand that the Department of National Health and Welfare has had report forms made so that doctors in various provinces can fill in those reports and report those cases.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is to the dominion bureau of statistics.
Will the minister let me say what I have to say?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am just trying to be helpful.
There is nothing like listening to an expert.
Well, if my hon. friend wanted to get the information perhaps he could be an expert, too. I imagine he is an expert in certain lines.
If you wish to go farther, yes.
At least he leads us to believe that he would want information. I do not want help from anyone who does not know anything about it. I am trying to get information from the minister.

Accept
information from any place you can get it.

Yes, if I consider it correct.
I have here the report of the Department of National Health and Welfare which sent out forms. All the provinces but one filled in those forms, and it is from them the bureau of statistics got their information. Does the minister say that next year, when he makes out his report, he is not going to give the people of Canada any information on the point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I did not say that.
That is exactly what the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend is one of the fairest members in the house. I know he would not say that. I am not refusing. But I am not going to give information, the full authenticity and completeness of which I am not satisfied with. I cannot say more than that at this time.
